old: As it happened, the boy’s relatives on his mother’s side forgot him too, at first. His grandfather was dead. His widow, Mitya’s grandmother, had moved to Moscow and was gravely ill. The daughters were all married. So for almost a year Mitya stayed with old Grigory and lived with him in the servant’s cottage. Even if his father had remembered him (he could hardly have been altogether unaware that the boy existed), he would have sent him back to the cottage anyway, since a child would only have got in the way of his debauchery. Then a cousin of Mitya’s mother, Pyotr Alexandrovitch Miüsov, returned from Paris. He lived abroad for many years afterwards, but at that time he was quite a young man and was known among the Miüsovs as a man of enlightened ideas and European culture, who had lived in the capitals and abroad. Late in life he became a Liberal of the kind common in the forties and fifties. Over his career he had met many of the most Liberal men of his day, in Russia and abroad. He had known Proudhon and Bakunin personally. In his old age he loved to describe the three days of the Paris Revolution of February 1848, hinting that he had very nearly fought on the barricades himself. It was one of the fondest memories of his youth. He owned an independent property of about a thousand souls, reckoning in the old way. His splendid estate lay on the edge of our little town and bordered the lands of our famous monastery. Almost as soon as he inherited it, Pyotr Alexandrovitch started an endless lawsuit against the monastery over fishing rights in the river or wood-cutting in the forest, I don’t know which. He saw it as his duty, as a citizen and a man of culture, to open an attack on the “clericals.” He heard the whole story of Adelaïda Ivanovna, whom, of course, he remembered, and in whom he had once taken an interest. When he learned that Mitya existed, he stepped in, for all his youthful indignation and contempt for Fyodor Pavlovitch. He met Fyodor Pavlovitch for the first time and told him bluntly that he wanted to take over the child’s education. Long afterwards he used to tell, as a telling detail, that when he began to speak of Mitya, Fyodor Pavlovitch stared for some time as if he didn’t understand which child was meant, and even seemed surprised to hear he had a little son in the house. The story may be exaggerated, but it must have been something like the truth.

old: As it turned out, the old lady died soon afterward, but in her will she left the boys a thousand roubles each “for their instruction, and so that all be spent on them exclusively, with the condition that it be so portioned out as to last till they are twenty-one, for it is more than adequate provision for such children. If other people think fit to throw away their money, let them.” I have not read the will myself, but I heard that there was something odd of the kind in it, very whimsically worded. The main heir was Yefim Petrovitch Polenov, the Marshal of Nobility of the province, and he proved to be an honest man. He wrote to Fyodor Pavlovitch and saw right away that there was nothing to be got out of him for the children’s education. (Fyodor Pavlovitch never actually said no, but only stalled, as he always did in such cases, and was even, at times, gushingly sentimental.) So Yefim Petrovitch took an interest in the orphans himself. He grew especially fond of the younger one, Alexey, who lived for a long time as a member of his family. I ask the reader to note this from the start. The young people owed their schooling and upbringing to Yefim Petrovitch more than to anyone else. He was a man of a generosity and humanity one rarely meets. He left the two thousand roubles that the general’s widow had left them untouched, so that by the time they came of age, the interest had doubled their shares. He paid for both their educations out of his own pocket, and he certainly spent far more than a thousand roubles on each. I will not give a detailed account of their boyhood and youth, only a few of the most important events. About the elder, Ivan, I will say only that he grew into a rather sullen, reserved boy, though far from timid. At ten he had understood that they lived not in their own home but on other people’s charity, and that their father was a man it was shameful to speak of. From very early on, almost from infancy (so they say, at least), the boy showed a brilliant and unusual talent for learning. I don’t know exactly why, but he left Yefim Petrovitch’s family when he was barely thirteen, and went to a Moscow gymnasium, where he boarded with an experienced and famous teacher who was an old friend of Yefim Petrovitch. Ivan used to say later that it was all because of Yefim Petrovitch’s “ardor for good works.” Yefim Petrovitch was carried away by the idea that a boy of genius ought to be trained by a teacher of genius. But by the time the young man finished at the gymnasium and entered the university, neither Yefim Petrovitch nor this teacher was alive. Yefim Petrovitch had made no arrangement for paying out the tyrannical old lady’s legacy, which had grown from one thousand to two. The money was held up by the red tape that is unavoidable in Russia, and for his first two years at the university the young man was hard pressed, because he had to keep himself the whole time he was studying. It should be noted that he did not even try to contact his father. Perhaps this was pride, or contempt. Perhaps it was cool common sense, which told him he would get no real help from such a father. Whatever the reason, the young man was not at all downhearted, and he found work. At first he gave lessons at sixpence an hour, and later he placed short items about street incidents in the newspapers, signed “Eye-Witness.” These items, it was said, were so lively and spicy that the papers soon took them. This alone showed the young man’s practical and intellectual superiority over the crowds of needy, unlucky students of both sexes who haunt the offices of newspapers and journals, unable to think of anything better than endless begging for copying work and translations from the French. Once Ivan Fyodorovitch had made contact with the editors, he always kept it up. In his later years at the university he published brilliant reviews of books on various specialized subjects, and became well known in literary circles. But only in his last year did he suddenly catch the attention of a much wider readership, so that a great many people noticed him and remembered him. It was a rather curious episode. He had just left the university and was getting ready to go abroad on his two thousand roubles, when Ivan Fyodorovitch published a strange article in one of the major journals. It attracted general notice. The subject was one he could have been supposed to know nothing about, since he was a student of natural science. It dealt with a question being debated everywhere at the time: the status of the ecclesiastical courts. After going through several opinions on the matter, he went on to give his own view. What struck people most about the article was its tone and its unexpected conclusion. Many in the Church party took him without question as one of their own. Yet the secularists, and even atheists, joined them in applauding him. In the end, some shrewd people suggested that the article was nothing but an impudent satirical burlesque. I mention this episode in particular because the article made its way into the famous monastery in our neighborhood. The monks there took a special interest in the question of the ecclesiastical courts, and the article left them completely bewildered. When they learned the author’s name, they were interested to find that he was a native of our town and the son of “that Fyodor Pavlovitch.” And just then the author himself showed up among us.

old: He was only twenty. His brother Ivan was in his twenty-fourth year at the time, and their eldest brother Dmitri was twenty-seven. First I must explain that this young man, Alyosha, was no fanatic and, in my opinion at least, not even a mystic. I may as well state my whole opinion at the outset. He was simply a lover of humanity from early on. He took up the monastic life only because, at that time, it struck him as the ideal way out for his soul, which was struggling up from the darkness of worldly wickedness toward the light of love. It struck him that way because he believed he had found in the monastery an extraordinary being, our celebrated elder, Zossima, and he had attached himself to Zossima with all the warm first love of his ardent heart. I don’t deny that he was very strange even then, and had been since the cradle. I have mentioned already that he lost his mother when he was four, yet remembered her all his life—her face, her caresses, “as though she stood living before me.” Such memories can reach back, as everyone knows, even to the age of two. But they seldom last a whole lifetime as isolated spots of light in the darkness, like the one corner left of a huge picture that has faded and vanished everywhere else. That is how it was with him. He remembered a still summer evening and an open window, with the slanting rays of the setting sun (that he recalled most vividly of all). In a corner of the room was the holy image with a lighted lamp before it, and on her knees in front of the image was his mother, sobbing hysterically, crying and moaning. She snatched him up in both arms and squeezed him so tight it hurt, and prayed for him to the Mother of God, holding him out in both arms toward the image as if to place him under the Mother’s protection ... and suddenly a nurse runs in and snatches him away from her in terror. That was the picture! And Alyosha remembered his mother’s face at that moment. He used to say it was frenzied but beautiful, as he remembered it. He rarely wanted to speak of this memory to anyone, though. As a child and a youth he was far from outgoing, and he talked very little. That was not from shyness or a sullen dislike of company. It was from something else, a kind of inner preoccupation, wholly his own and having nothing to do with other people, yet so important to him that it made him seem to forget them. But he was fond of people. All his life he seemed to trust people completely, and still no one ever thought him a simpleton or naïve. Something about him made you feel at once (and this held true all his life) that he had no wish to sit in judgment on others—that he would never presume to criticize, and would never condemn anyone for anything. He seemed, in fact, to accept everything without the least condemnation, although he often grieved bitterly. So thoroughly was this so, that even in his earliest youth nothing could surprise or frighten him. At twenty he came to his father’s house, a perfect sink of filthy debauchery. Chaste and pure as he was, he simply withdrew in silence whenever the sight became unbearable, and he showed no sign of contempt or condemnation. His father had once lived as a dependent himself, so he was touchy and quick to take offense, and he received Alyosha at first with distrust and sullenness. “He doesn’t say much,” he would say, “and he thinks the more.” But soon—within two weeks, in fact—he was embracing and kissing Alyosha terribly often, with drunken tears and sottish sentimentality. Still, he plainly felt a real and deep affection for him, the like of which he had never been capable of feeling for anyone before.

old: Everyone, in fact, loved this young man wherever he went, and that had been so since his earliest childhood. When he entered the household of his patron and benefactor, Yefim Petrovitch Polenov, he won the hearts of the whole family, who came to look on him quite as their own child. Yet he went to live there at such a tender age that he could not have been calculating or scheming to win affection. The gift of being loved, immediately and without any effort, was simply inborn in him, part of his nature, so to speak. It was the same at school, though he seemed exactly the sort of child that other children distrust, sometimes ridicule, and even dislike. He was dreamy, for example, and rather solitary. From his earliest years he loved to creep into a corner and read, and yet he was a general favorite all the time he was at school. He was seldom playful or merry, but you could see at a glance that this was not sullenness. On the contrary, he was cheerful and good-tempered. He never tried to show off among his schoolmates. Perhaps for that reason, he was afraid of no one, yet the boys realized at once that he took no pride in his fearlessness and seemed not to know he was bold and brave. He never resented an insult. An hour after being wronged, he might speak to the one who had done it, or answer his question, with a look as trusting and open as if nothing had passed between them. It was not that he seemed to have forgotten the insult, or made up his mind to forgive it. He simply did not count it as an insult, and this completely won over the boys and captivated them. He had one trait that made all his schoolmates, from the lowest class to the highest, want to mock him—not out of malice, but because it amused them. That trait was a wild, fanatical modesty and chastity. He could not stand to hear certain words and certain talk about women. Unhappily, there are “certain” words and talk that no one can stamp out in schools. Boys who are pure in mind and heart, hardly more than children, love to discuss among themselves, and even out loud, things and pictures and images that even soldiers would think twice about mentioning. More than that, much that soldiers know nothing of is familiar to quite small children of our educated and upper classes. It isn’t moral depravity, or any real inner corruption and cynicism, but it has the look of those, and among the boys it is often considered refined, subtle, daring, and worth copying. When they saw Alyosha Karamazov stick his fingers in his ears whenever they talked of “that,” they would sometimes crowd around him, pull his hands away, and shout filth into both his ears. He would struggle, slip down onto the floor, and try to hide, without saying one word of abuse, and endure their insults in silence. In the end, though, they left him alone and stopped teasing him as a “regular girl.” What’s more, they came to view it with pity, as a weakness. In class he was always among the best, but never first.

old: Some of my readers may imagine that my young man was a sickly, ecstatic, underdeveloped creature, a pale, consumptive dreamer. Quite the opposite: at this time Alyosha was a sturdy, red-cheeked, clear-eyed lad of nineteen, glowing with health. He was very handsome, too. He was graceful and moderately tall, with dark brown hair and a regular, rather long, oval face. His dark gray eyes were wide-set and shining. He was very thoughtful and seemed very serene. I will be told, perhaps, that red cheeks do not rule out fanaticism and mysticism. But I think Alyosha was more of a realist than anyone. Oh, no doubt in the monastery he fully believed in miracles, but to my mind miracles never trouble a realist. It is not miracles that lead realists to belief. The true realist, if he is an unbeliever, will always find the strength and ability to disbelieve in the miraculous. Faced with a miracle as an undeniable fact, he would sooner doubt his own senses than accept it. And if he does accept it, he accepts it as a fact of nature that he had simply not recognized before. In the realist, faith does not spring from the miracle; the miracle springs from faith. Once a realist believes, his very realism obliges him to admit the miraculous too. The Apostle Thomas said he would not believe until he saw, but when he did see, he said, “My Lord and my God!” Was it the miracle that forced him to believe? Most likely not. He believed only because he wanted to believe, and perhaps in his secret heart he fully believed even when he said, “I do not believe till I see.”

old: I will be told, perhaps, that Alyosha was stupid, undeveloped, that he had not finished his studies, and so on. It is true that he did not finish his studies, but to call him stupid or dull would be a great injustice. I will simply repeat what I said above. He chose this path only because at that time it alone struck his imagination, and it offered his soul an ideal escape from darkness into light. Add to that that he was, to some extent, a young man of our last epoch. That is, he was honest by nature. He wanted the truth, sought it and believed in it, and wanted to serve it at once with all the strength of his soul. He looked for immediate action and was ready to sacrifice everything for it, even life itself. Unfortunately, these young men fail to understand that sacrificing one’s life is, in many cases, the easiest of all sacrifices. They do not see that it might mean giving up five or six years of their seething youth to hard and tedious study, if only to multiply tenfold their power to serve the truth and the cause they have set as their goal. Such a sacrifice is utterly beyond the strength of many of them. The path Alyosha chose ran in the opposite direction, but he chose it with the same thirst for swift achievement. As soon as he thought seriously, he was convinced that God and immortality exist, and at once he said to himself, instinctively: “I want to live for immortality, and I will accept no compromise.” In the same way, if he had decided that God and immortality did not exist, he would at once have become an atheist and a socialist. For socialism is not merely the labor question. It is above all the atheistic question, the question of the form atheism takes today, the question of the tower of Babel built without God, not to climb from earth to heaven but to bring heaven down to earth. Alyosha would have found it strange and impossible to go on living as before. It is written: “Give all that thou hast to the poor and follow Me, if thou wouldst be perfect.”
new: I will be told, perhaps, that Alyosha was stupid, undeveloped, that he had not finished his studies, and so on. It is true that he did not finish his studies, but to call him stupid or dull would be a great injustice. I will simply repeat what I said above. He chose this path only because at that time it alone struck his imagination, and it offered his soul an ideal escape from darkness into light. Add to that that he was, to some extent, a young man of our last epoch. That is, he was honest by nature. He wanted the truth, sought it and believed in it, and wanted to serve it at once with all the strength of his soul. He looked for immediate action and was ready to sacrifice everything for it, even life itself. Unfortunately, these young men fail to understand that sacrificing one’s life is, in many cases, the easiest of all sacrifices, and that to sacrifice, for instance, five or six years of their seething youth to hard and tedious study, if only to multiply tenfold their power to serve the truth and the cause they have set as their goal, is a sacrifice utterly beyond the strength of many of them. The path Alyosha chose ran in the opposite direction, but he chose it with the same thirst for swift achievement. As soon as he thought seriously, he was convinced that God and immortality exist, and at once he said to himself, instinctively: “I want to live for immortality, and I will accept no compromise.” In the same way, if he had decided that God and immortality did not exist, he would at once have become an atheist and a socialist. For socialism is not merely the labor question. It is above all the atheistic question, the question of the form atheism takes today, the question of the tower of Babel built without God, not to climb from earth to heaven but to bring heaven down to earth. Alyosha would have found it strange and impossible to go on living as before. It is written: “Give all that thou hast to the poor and follow Me, if thou wouldst be perfect.”

old: It was at this time that the meeting, or rather the gathering, of this ill-matched family took place in the cell of the elder, who had such an extraordinary influence over Alyosha. The occasion for it was a false one. The quarrel between Dmitri and his father seemed to be at its worst just then, and relations between them had become unbearably strained. Fyodor Pavlovitch seems to have been the first to propose, apparently as a joke, that they should all meet in Father Zossima’s cell. They need not ask the elder to step in, he said, but they could settle things more decently with the soothing effect of his presence. Dmitri had never seen the elder. He naturally supposed that his father was trying to intimidate him. But he secretly blamed himself for losing his temper with his father several times lately, and so he accepted the challenge. It should be noted that he did not stay with his father, as Ivan did, but lived apart at the other end of the town. It happened that Pyotr Alexandrovitch Miüsov, who was staying in the district at that time, seized eagerly on the idea. He was a Liberal of the forties and fifties, a freethinker and an atheist, and he may have been driven by boredom or by the hope of some idle amusement. Suddenly he wanted to see the monastery and the holy man. His lawsuit with the monastery was still dragging on, and he made that his excuse to call on the Superior and try to settle it on friendly terms. A visitor with such praiseworthy intentions might get a warmer, more attentive reception than one who came out of simple curiosity. Pressure was put on the elder from inside the monastery. He had hardly left his cell lately, and illness had forced him to turn away even his usual visitors. In the end he agreed to see them, and the day was set.

old: They entered the room almost at the same moment that the elder came in from his bedroom. Two monks of the hermitage were already waiting in the cell: the Father Librarian, and Father Païssy, who was said to be very learned and was in poor health, though not old. A tall young man of about twenty-two also stood in the corner, and stayed there for the whole visit. His face was broad and fresh, his narrow brown eyes clever and watchful, and his clothes were ordinary. He was a divinity student living under the monastery’s protection. He looked reverent without question, yet with self-respect. His position was dependent and beneath the guests’, so he did not bow to them.

old: “Great elder, tell me! Does my liveliness annoy you?” Fyodor Pavlovitch cried suddenly. He gripped the arms of his chair with both hands, as if he meant to jump up and run if the answer was a bad one.

old: “Entirely at home? To be my natural self? Oh, that’s much too generous, but I take it with grateful joy. You know, blessed Father, you’d better not invite me to be my natural self. Don’t risk it.... I won’t go so far myself. I’m warning you for your own good. As for the rest, it’s still lost in the mists of uncertainty, though there are people who’d be delighted to describe me to you. I mean that for you, Pyotr Alexandrovitch. But you, holy being, I tell you, I’m simply overflowing with ecstasy.”

old: “No, not about Diderot. Above all, do not lie to yourself. A man who lies to himself and listens to his own lie comes to a point where he cannot tell the truth in himself or around him, and so he loses all respect for himself and for others. Having no respect, he stops loving. And to keep himself occupied and distracted without love, he gives himself up to passions and coarse pleasures, and in his vices he sinks to the level of a beast. All of this comes from lying continually to other men and to himself. The man who lies to himself is also more easily offended than anyone. You know, it is sometimes very pleasant to take offense, is it not? A man may know that no one has insulted him, that he has invented the insult himself, lied and exaggerated to make it picturesque, seized on one word and made a mountain out of a molehill. He knows all this, and still he is the first to take offense. He revels in his resentment until it gives him great pleasure, and so he passes to real vindictiveness. But get up, sit down, please. All this, too, is deceitful posturing....”

old: The elder suddenly stood up. “Excuse me, gentlemen, if I leave you for a few minutes,” he said to all his guests. “There are visitors waiting for me who came before you. But do not tell lies all the same,” he added to Fyodor Pavlovitch, with a good-humored face. He left the cell, and Alyosha and the novice hurried after him to help him down the steps. Alyosha was out of breath. He was glad to get away, but glad too that the elder was in good humor and not offended. Father Zossima was heading for the portico to bless the people waiting there. But Fyodor Pavlovitch stubbornly stopped him at the door of the cell.

old: Father Zossima came into the portico, but he did not go to the ladies first. He went straight to the peasants who were crowded at the bottom of the three steps up to it. He stood on the top step, put on his stole, and began blessing the women as they pressed around him. A crazy woman was brought up to him. The moment she saw the elder, she began to shriek and writhe as if in the pains of childbirth. He laid the stole on her forehead and said a short prayer over her, and at once she grew calm and quiet.

old: I do not know how it is now, but in my childhood I often saw and heard these “possessed” women in villages and monasteries. They were brought to mass, and there they would squeal and bark like dogs so loudly that the whole church heard them. But when the sacrament was carried in and they were led up to it, the “possession” stopped at once, and for a while the sick women were always calm. As a child I was deeply impressed and amazed by this. Then I heard from our country neighbors and from my teachers in town that the whole illness was faked to get out of work, and that firm enough treatment could always cure it. They told various stories to prove it. Later, though, medical specialists told me, to my astonishment, that nothing is faked here. It is a terrible illness that women suffer from, and it is especially widespread in Russia. It comes, they said, from the hard lot of peasant women. A woman goes back to exhausting work too soon after a difficult, unnatural childbirth with no help. Add hopeless misery and beatings and the like, which some women could not bear as well as others. So the strange, instant cure of the frantic, struggling woman as soon as she was brought to the holy sacrament had been explained to me as malingering and the trickery of the “clericals.” In fact, it probably came about in the most natural way. The women who held her up, and the sick woman herself, were completely certain that the evil spirit inside her could not hold out once she was brought to the sacrament and made to bow down before it. So in a nervous, mentally disturbed woman, the whole body went into a sort of convulsion, and it was bound to, at the moment of bowing down. The expectation of a miraculous cure and the unquestioning belief that it would come set it off. And it did come, though only for a moment. It was exactly the same now, as soon as the elder touched the sick woman with the stole.

old: “Are you telling the truth? Well, then, after such a confession I believe that you are sincere and good at heart. If you do not find happiness, always remember that you are on the right road, and try not to leave it. Above all, avoid falsehood, every kind of falsehood, especially falseness toward yourself. Watch your own deceitfulness and examine it every hour, every minute. Avoid scorn, toward others and toward yourself. What seems bad in you will grow purer simply because you see it in yourself. Avoid fear too, though fear is only the consequence of every sort of falsehood. Never be frightened by your own weakness in pursuing love. Do not be too frightened even by your evil actions. I am sorry I can say nothing more consoling to you, for love in action is a harsh and dreadful thing compared with love in dreams. Love in dreams is greedy for immediate action, quickly done and seen by all. People will even give their lives, if only the trial does not last long but is soon over, with everyone watching and applauding as if at a play. But active love is labor and endurance, and for some people, perhaps, a whole science. But I predict that just when you see with horror that, in spite of all your efforts, you are moving farther from your goal and not closer to it—at that very moment, I predict, you will reach it. You will see clearly the miraculous power of the Lord, who has loved you all along and has been guiding you in secret. Forgive me, I cannot stay longer with you. They are waiting for me. Goodbye.”

old: The elder had been out of his cell for about twenty-five minutes. It was already past half-past twelve, and Dmitri, the reason they had all gathered there, still had not appeared. He seemed almost forgotten, though, and when the elder came back in, he found his guests deep in lively conversation. Ivan and the two monks were doing most of the talking. Miüsov was trying to take part too, and quite eagerly, it seemed. But he had no luck at that either. He was plainly pushed into the background, and his remarks were ignored, which only made him more irritable. He had crossed swords with Ivan before, and he could not stand a certain offhandedness Ivan showed toward him.

old: “Let me ask your permission to drop this subject altogether,” Miüsov repeated. “Instead, gentlemen, I’ll tell you another interesting and fairly typical story about Ivan Fyodorovitch himself. Just five days ago, at a gathering here, mostly of ladies, he announced in the middle of an argument that nothing in the whole world makes people love their neighbors. He said there is no natural law that man should love mankind. If there has been any love on earth up to now, he said, it was not because of a natural law but only because men have believed in immortality. Ivan Fyodorovitch added in passing that the whole of natural law rests on that belief. Destroy mankind’s faith in immortality, he said, and not only love but every living force that keeps the world going would dry up at once. Moreover, nothing would be immoral then, and everything would be lawful, even cannibalism. And that’s not all. He finished by claiming that for every individual like ourselves, who believes neither in God nor in immortality, the natural moral law must at once turn into the exact opposite of the old religious law. Egoism, even to the point of crime, would become not merely lawful but recognized as the inevitable, the most rational, even the most honorable outcome of his situation. From this one paradox, gentlemen, you can judge the rest of the theories of our eccentric and paradoxical friend Ivan Fyodorovitch.”

old: “Speak without clowning, and don’t begin by insulting your own family,” answered the elder, in a weak, worn-out voice. He was plainly growing more and more tired, and his strength was failing.

old: “I thought ... I thought,” he said, in a soft, almost controlled voice, “that I was coming home with the angel of my heart, my betrothed, to look after his old age. And all I find is a depraved libertine and a despicable clown!”

old: But this shameful scene was ended in the most unexpected way. Father Zossima suddenly rose from his seat. Alyosha was nearly frantic with worry for the elder and for everyone else, but he managed to hold him up by the arm. Father Zossima walked toward Dmitri, and when he reached him he sank to his knees. Alyosha thought he had fallen from weakness, but he had not. The elder bowed down at Dmitri’s feet, slowly and deliberately, until his forehead touched the floor. Alyosha was so astonished that he did not help him up again. There was a faint smile on the elder’s lips.

old: “Of course I mean you,” cried Fyodor Pavlovitch. “Who else? The Father Superior can hardly be von Sohn.”

old: “Tut—tut—tut—pious talk and stock phrases! Old phrases and old gestures. The same old lies and ceremonial kowtowing. We know all about it. A kiss on the lips and a dagger in the heart, like in Schiller’s _Robbers_. I don’t like falsehood, Fathers. I want the truth. But the truth isn’t found in eating gudgeon, and I say so out loud! Father monks, why do you fast? Why do you expect a reward in heaven for it? For a reward like that, I’ll come and fast myself! No, saintly monk, you try being virtuous out in the world. Do some good for society, without locking yourself in a monastery at other people’s expense and without hoping for a reward up above—you’ll find that a bit harder. I can talk sense too, Father Superior. What have they got here?” He went up to the table. “Old port wine, and mead brewed by the Eliseyev Brothers. Fie, fie, Fathers! That’s a long way past gudgeon. Look at the bottles the fathers have set out, he he he! And who paid for all this? The Russian peasant, the working man, brings the farthing he earned with his horny hand, wrung from his family and the tax collector! You bleed the people, you know, holy fathers.”

old: “I was living wildly in those days. Father said just now that I spent several thousand roubles on seducing young girls. That’s a filthy invention. Nothing of the sort happened. And if it did, I didn’t need money for _that_. For me, money is a trimming, the overflow of my heart, the stage set. One day she’d be my lady; the next, some girl from the street would be in her place. I entertained them both. I tossed money away by the fistful on music, wild parties and gypsies. Sometimes I handed it to the ladies too, since they grab it eagerly, I have to admit, and are pleased and thankful for it. Ladies were fond of me. Not every one, but it happened, it happened. Still, I always preferred the side-paths, the little dark back-alleys off the main road. That’s where the adventures are, and the surprises, and the precious metal in the dirt. I’m talking figuratively, brother. The town I lived in had no back-alleys like that in the literal sense, but morally it had plenty. If you were like me, you’d know what I mean. I loved vice. I loved the disgrace of vice. I loved cruelty. Am I not a bug, a noxious insect? A Karamazov, in a word! Once a whole crowd of us drove out on a picnic, in seven sledges. It was winter and dark, and I began squeezing a girl’s hand and forced her to kiss me. She was the daughter of an official, a sweet, gentle, yielding creature. In the dark she let me do a great deal. She thought, poor thing, that I’d come the next day and propose. (I was thought a good catch, too.) But for five months I didn’t say one word to her. At dances (we had dances all the time) I would see her in a corner with her eyes on me. I saw them glow with a fire, a fire of gentle indignation. This game just tickled the insect lust I kept in my soul. Five months later she married an official and left town, still angry, and still, perhaps, in love with me. Now they’re happy together. Note that I told nobody. I didn’t brag about it. I’m full of low desires and I love what’s low, but I’m not dishonorable. You’re blushing; your eyes flashed. That’s enough of this filth with you. And all that was nothing much, wayside blossoms _à la_ Paul de Kock, though the cruel insect had already grown strong in my soul. I’ve a whole album of memories, brother. God bless them, the darlings. I always tried to part without a quarrel. And I never gave them away. I never bragged about even one. But enough of that. You can’t think I brought you here only to talk such nonsense. No. What I’m going to tell you is more curious. And don’t be surprised that I’m glad to tell it, instead of being ashamed.”

old: “I was a lieutenant in a line regiment, but I was still watched, like a sort of convict. Even so, the little town received me awfully well. I spent money left and right. People took me for rich, and so did I. But I must have charmed them in other ways too. They shook their heads over me, yet they liked me. My colonel, an old man, suddenly took against me. He was forever picking on me. But I had powerful friends, and the whole town besides was on my side, so he couldn’t do me much harm. Partly it was my own fault, since I wouldn’t show him proper respect. I was proud. This stubborn old fellow was really a very decent sort, kind-hearted and hospitable. He’d had two wives, and both were dead. His first wife, from a humble family, left a daughter as unpretentious as herself. When I was there she was a young woman of twenty-four. She lived with her father and an aunt, her mother’s sister. The aunt was simple and had no schooling; the niece was simple too, but lively. I like saying nice things about people. I never knew a woman with a more charming nature than Agafya. Imagine, her name was Agafya Ivanovna! And she wasn’t bad-looking either, in the Russian way: tall, stout, with a full figure and beautiful eyes, though her face was rather coarse. She’d never married, though two men had asked her. She said no to both and stayed as cheerful as ever. We were close, though not in ‘that’ way. It was pure friendship. I’ve often been friends with women quite innocently. I talked to her with shocking frankness, and she only laughed. Many women enjoy such freedom, and since she was a girl as well, it was very amusing. And another thing: you could never think of her as a young lady. She and her aunt lived in her father’s house with a kind of chosen humility, never setting themselves up as equal to other people. Everyone liked her and she was useful to all, being a clever dressmaker. She had a talent for it. She gave her work freely, asking for nothing, but if someone offered to pay, she didn’t say no. The colonel, of course, was another matter altogether. He was one of the leading figures of the district. He kept open house and entertained the whole town, with suppers and dances. When I arrived and joined the battalion, the whole town was talking about the colonel’s second daughter, a great beauty, who was expected home any day. She had just left a fashionable school in the capital. This second daughter is Katerina Ivanovna. She was the child of the second wife, who came from the family of a distinguished general. Though, as I learned on good authority, she too brought the colonel no money. She had connections, and that was all. There may have been expectations, but they had come to nothing.

old: “Meanwhile I passed my time in drink and riot, until the lieutenant-colonel put me under arrest for three days. Right then father sent me six thousand roubles. In return I’d sent him a deed giving up all claims on him—settling our accounts, so to speak, and saying I’d expect nothing more. I didn’t understand a word of it then. Until I came here, Alyosha, until the last few days really, and maybe even now, I haven’t been able to make head or tail of my money affairs with father. But never mind that. We’ll talk about it later.

old: “But how can you?”
new: “But is that possible?”

old: “To Grushenka, then!” Alyosha exclaimed sadly, wringing his hands. “So Rakitin did tell the truth! I thought you’d only called on her, and that was all.”
new: “To Grushenka, then!” Alyosha exclaimed sadly, clasping his hands. “Can Rakitin really have told the truth? I thought you’d only called on her, and that was all.”

old: “Mitya, you are unhappy, yes! But not as unhappy as you think. Don’t kill yourself with despair.”
new: “Mitya, you are unhappy, yes! But not as unhappy as you think. Don’t torment yourself to death with despair.”

old: “I know he won’t. I know it perfectly well, and now more than ever. And that’s not all. I know something else. Only a few days ago, perhaps just yesterday, he understood for the first time _in earnest_ (underline _in earnest_) that Grushenka may not be joking after all, and really means to marry me. He knows what she’s like; he knows the cat. So do you imagine he’ll give me money to help that along, when he’s mad about her himself? And that isn’t all, either. I can tell you more than that. I know that for the past five days he’s had three thousand drawn from the bank, changed into notes of a hundred roubles, packed into a big envelope, sealed with five seals and tied crosswise with red tape. You see how well informed I am! On the envelope he’s written: ‘To my angel Grushenka, if she will come to me.’ He scrawled it himself, silently and in secret, and nobody knows the money is there except the valet Smerdyakov, whom he trusts as he trusts himself. So for three or four days now he’s been expecting Grushenka. He hopes she’ll come for the money. He’s sent word to her about it, and she’s sent word back that perhaps she’ll come. And if she does go to the old man, can I marry her afterwards? Now you see why I’m here in secret, and what I’m keeping watch for.”

old: When Fyodor Pavlovitch heard how Smerdyakov was turning out, he made up his mind to have him as his cook, and sent him to Moscow to train. He stayed there some years and came back strikingly changed in looks. He seemed extraordinarily old for his age. His face had gone wrinkled and yellow, and oddly like a eunuch’s. In character he seemed almost exactly as he had been before leaving. He was as unsociable as ever and showed not the slightest wish for company. In Moscow, too, as we heard afterwards, he had always kept silent. Moscow itself had little interest for him; he saw very little of it and noticed hardly anything. He went to the theater once, and came back quiet and put out by it. On the other hand, he returned to us from Moscow well dressed, in a clean coat and clean linen. Every day, without fail, he brushed his clothes with great care twice, and he loved cleaning his smart calf boots with a special English polish until they shone like mirrors. He turned out to be a first-rate cook. Fyodor Pavlovitch paid him a salary, and Smerdyakov spent nearly all of it on clothes, pomade, perfume and the like. But he seemed to hold women in just as much contempt as men. With them he was discreet, almost unapproachable. Fyodor Pavlovitch began to see him a little differently. The fits were coming more often, and on the days when he was ill Marfa cooked, which did not suit Fyodor Pavlovitch at all.

old: “Think it over for yourself, Grigory Vassilyevitch,” Smerdyakov went on, sedate and unruffled. He was aware of his triumph, yet, as it were, generous toward the beaten foe. “Think it over for yourself, Grigory Vassilyevitch. The Scripture says that if you have faith as small as a mustard seed and tell a mountain to move into the sea, it will move at your word without the slightest delay. Very well, Grigory Vassilyevitch. I am without faith, and you have so great a faith that you swear at me constantly. So you try it. Tell this mountain to move, not into the sea, which is a long way off, but just into our stinking little river at the bottom of the garden. You will see for yourself that it will not budge. It will stay exactly where it is, however much you shout at it. That shows, Grigory Vassilyevitch, that you do not have faith in the proper manner, and only abuse other people about it. Consider this as well. In our day nobody, not only you but actually nobody, from the highest gentleman to the lowest peasant, can push mountains into the sea—except perhaps one man in the whole world, or two at the most, and they are very likely saving their souls in secret somewhere in the Egyptian desert, so you would never find them. Now, if that is the case, and all the rest have no faith, will God curse all the rest? That is, the population of the entire earth, except for about two hermits in the desert? And in His well-known mercy, will He not forgive even one of them? And so I am convinced that although I may once have doubted, I shall be forgiven if I shed tears of repentance.”

old: “Every night after dinner Smerdyakov shoves his way in now. It’s you he’s so keen on. What have you done to charm him?” he added, to Ivan.

old: “Fine, I’ll go. You’ve had too much brandy.”
new: “Well, I’m leaving. You’ve had too much brandy.”

old: “What are you staring at me for? Why do you look like that? Your eyes look at me and say, ‘You filthy drunk!’ Your eyes don’t trust me. They’re full of contempt.... You’ve come here with some plan in mind. Now Alyosha looks at me and his eyes shine. Alyosha doesn’t despise me. Alexey, you mustn’t love Ivan.”

old: And he blew a loud kiss to his own hand.
new: And he kissed his hand with a loud smack.

old: “I’ve known about it for a long time. I telegraphed to Moscow to inquire, and heard long ago that the money had not come. He hadn’t sent it, but I said nothing. Last week I found out that he was still short of money. All I wanted in all this was for him to know whom to turn to, and who was his true friend. No, he won’t admit that I am his truest friend. He won’t know me. He looks on me only as a woman. I’ve been tormented all week, trying to think how to keep him from being ashamed to face me because he spent that three thousand. Let him be ashamed before himself, let him be ashamed of other people knowing, but not of my knowing. He can tell God everything without shame. Why is it that he still doesn’t understand how much I’m ready to bear for his sake? Why, why doesn’t he know me? How dare he not know me, after all that has happened? I want to save him forever. Let him forget me as his betrothed. And here he fears that he’s dishonored in my eyes. Why, he wasn’t afraid to be open with you, Alexey Fyodorovitch. Why do I not deserve the same?”

old: And he told her the whole scene: how Dmitri had sent him to get the money, how he himself had burst in and knocked his father down, and how after that he had again, specially and emphatically, begged Alyosha to carry her his compliments and his farewell. “He has gone to that woman,” Alyosha added softly.

old: “Yes, and maybe you misunderstand me completely too, dear young lady. Maybe I’m not as good as I seem to you. I have a bad heart. I like to get my own way. I charmed poor Dmitri Fyodorovitch that day just for fun.”

old: “Hold on. Look at the night. See how dark it is, the clouds, the wind that’s picked up. I was hiding under that willow, waiting for you. And I swear by God above, I suddenly thought: why drag on in misery any longer? What is there left to wait for? Here’s a willow, here’s a handkerchief, here’s a shirt. In a minute I can twist them into a rope, and I have my suspenders too. Why go on weighing down the earth and shaming it with my filthy presence? And then I heard you coming—heavens, it was as if something dropped down to me out of the sky. So there is someone I love after all! Here he is, my dear little brother, the one I love more than anyone in the world, the only one I love in the world. And at that moment I loved you so much, so much, that I thought, ‘I’ll throw myself on his neck this instant.’ Then a stupid notion came over me: play a joke on you, give you a scare. So I shouted that idiotic ‘Your money!’ Forgive the clowning—it was nonsense, nothing indecent is in my soul.... Damn it all, tell me what happened. What did she say? Hit me, crush me, show me no mercy! Was she furious?”

old: “Impossible!” he cried. “You’re raving! Grushenka, at her house?”

old: “Brother, you haven’t even noticed how badly you insulted Katerina Ivanovna by telling Grushenka about that day. And Grushenka threw it in her face just now: that she had gone to gentlemen in secret to sell her beauty! Brother, what insult could be worse than that?”

old: “Yes, maybe I did tell Grushenka about that ‘fatal day,’ as Katya calls it. Yes, I told her, I remember it now! It was at Mokroe. I was drunk, the gypsies were singing.... But I was sobbing. I was sobbing then, on my knees, praying to Katya’s image, and Grushenka understood. She understood everything then. I remember, she cried herself.... Damn it all! But it was bound to end this way.... Then she cried, and now it’s ‘the dagger in the heart’! That’s women for you.”

old: Now he was rather puzzled and did not know whom to believe. The evening before, he had visited Father Ferapont in his separate cell behind the apiary, and the visit had left him deeply impressed and awed. This Father Ferapont was the aged monk, devoted to fasting and silence, who has been mentioned already as opposed to Father Zossima and to the whole institution of “elders,” which he held to be a harmful and frivolous novelty. He was a formidable opponent, although his vow of silence meant he hardly spoke to anyone. He was formidable because a number of monks shared his feelings entirely, and many visitors saw him as a great saint and ascetic, even though they had no doubt he was crazy. Yet it was precisely his craziness that drew them.

old: “Is it me you want to bow down to, monk?” said Father Ferapont. “Get up!”

old: “He doesn’t ask for money, it’s true, but he’ll not get a farthing out of me all the same. I mean to live as long as I can, you may as well know, my dear Alexey Fyodorovitch, and so I need every farthing, and the longer I live, the more I’ll need,” he went on, pacing from one corner of the room to the other, his hands in the pockets of his loose, greasy overcoat of yellow cotton. “I can still pass for a man of fifty-five, but I want to go on passing for one another twenty years. The older I get, you know, the less pretty I’ll be. The wenches won’t come to me for nothing, so I’ll need my money. That’s why I’m saving up more and more, just for myself, my dear son Alexey Fyodorovitch. You may as well know that. Because I mean to go on sinning to the end, let me tell you. Sin is sweet. Everybody curses it, and everybody lives in it, only the others do it on the sly and I do it in the open. And that’s why all the other sinners jump on me, for being so simple. And your paradise, Alexey Fyodorovitch, isn’t to my taste, let me tell you. It’s no place for a gentleman, your paradise, even if there is such a thing. I believe I fall asleep and never wake up, and that’s the end of it. Pray for my soul if you like. If you don’t want to, then don’t, damn you! That’s my philosophy. Ivan spoke well here yesterday, though we were all drunk. Ivan is a conceited coxcomb, but he has no great learning ... no education either. He sits there silent, smiling at you and saying nothing—that’s what gets him by.”

old: “One reptile will eat the other,” Ivan had said the day before, speaking angrily of their father and Dmitri. So Ivan saw Dmitri as a reptile, and perhaps had for a long time. Perhaps ever since he had known Katerina Ivanovna? Of course, the phrase had slipped out of Ivan yesterday without his meaning it, but that only made it more important. If he felt that way, what hope was there of peace? Were there not, rather, fresh grounds for hatred and hostility in their family? And whose side was Alyosha to take? And what was he to wish for each of them? He loved them both. But what could he wish for either one, with their interests clashing like this? He could lose his way completely in this maze, and Alyosha’s heart could not stand uncertainty, because his love was always active. He could not love passively. When he loved someone, he set to work at once to help him. To do that, he had to know what he was aiming at. He had to know for certain what was best for each of them, and once he knew, it came naturally to him to help them both. But instead of a clear aim, he found only uncertainty and confusion on every side. “It was lacerating,” as had just been said. But what could he make of even this “laceration”? He could not understand the first word of this baffling maze.

old: “Never mind that it’s honestly come by, from a ‘sister’ I respect and revere so highly. Do you know, I can now look after mamma and Nina, my hunchback angel of a daughter? Doctor Herzenstube came to see us, out of the goodness of his heart, and spent a whole hour examining the two of them. ‘I can’t make anything of it,’ he said. But he prescribed a mineral water, sold at the chemist’s here. He said it would surely do her good, and he ordered baths as well, with some medicine in the water. The mineral water costs thirty kopecks a bottle, and she might need forty of them. So I took the prescription, put it on the shelf under the ikons, and there it lies. And for Nina he ordered hot baths, with something dissolved in them, morning and evening. But how are we to manage a cure like that in our mansion? We have no servants, no help, no bath, not even any water! Nina has rheumatism all over, I don’t think I mentioned that. At night her whole right side aches. She’s in agony, and would you believe it, the angel suffers without a groan, so as not to wake us. We eat whatever we can find, and she will take only the scraps, what you’d hardly throw to a dog. ‘I don’t deserve it, I’m taking it from you, I’m a burden to you,’ that’s what her angel eyes are trying to say. We wait on her, but she hates it. ‘I’m a useless cripple, good for nothing.’ As if she didn’t deserve it, when she is what saves all of us, with her angelic sweetness! Without her, without her gentle word, it would be hell among us! She softens even Varvara. And don’t judge Varvara harshly either. She’s an angel too, and she’s been wronged too. She came to us for the summer with sixteen roubles she had saved from giving lessons, meant for her trip back to Petersburg in September, which is now. But we took her money and lived on it, so now she has nothing to go back with. Not that she could go back anyway, since she has to slave for us here. She’s like an overworked horse with all of us riding on her back. She waits on everyone, mends, washes, sweeps the floor, puts mamma to bed. And mamma is fretful and tearful and out of her mind! But now, with this money, I can hire a servant, you understand, Alexey Fyodorovitch. I can buy medicines for the dear creatures. I can send my student to Petersburg. I can buy beef and feed them properly. Good Lord, it’s a dream!”

old: And then he ran on without looking back. Alyosha watched him go, grieved beyond words. Oh, he saw that until the very last moment the man had not known he would crush the notes and throw them away. The captain did not turn back, and Alyosha knew he would not. He would not follow or call him back, and he knew why. When the man was out of sight, Alyosha picked up the two notes. They were badly crumpled and had been ground into the sand, but they were not torn. They even rustled like new ones when Alyosha unfolded and smoothed them out. Once he had smoothed them, he folded them, put them in his pocket, and went to Katerina Ivanovna to report on how her errand had turned out.

old: “Because if he’d taken the money, an hour after getting home he’d be weeping with mortification. That’s exactly what would have happened. And most likely he’d have come to me first thing tomorrow and maybe thrown the notes at me and trampled on them, as he did just now. But now he’s gone home terribly proud and triumphant, even though he knows he’s ‘ruined himself.’ So now nothing could be easier than getting him to accept the two hundred roubles by tomorrow, because he’s already proved his honor, tossed the money away and stamped on it.... He couldn’t know, when he did it, that I’d bring it to him again tomorrow, and yet he’s in terrible need of that money. Proud as he is of himself now, even today he’ll be thinking what help he’s thrown away. At night he’ll think about it more than ever and dream about it, and by tomorrow morning he may be ready to run to me and beg my forgiveness. And that’s just when I’ll turn up. ‘Look, you’re a proud man,’ I’ll say. ‘You’ve shown it; but now take the money and forgive us!’ And then he’ll take it!”

old: “I could have gone further than this. I could have known more, if my fate hadn’t been against me from childhood. I would have shot a man in a duel for calling me names because my mother was a filthy beggar and I have no father. In Moscow they used to throw that in my teeth. The story had reached them from here, thanks to Grigory Vassilyevitch. Grigory Vassilyevitch accuses me of rebelling against my birth, but I would have agreed to their killing me before I was born, so that I would never have come into the world at all. In the market they used to say it, and your mamma too, with a great want of delicacy, began telling me that her hair was like a mat on her head and that she was short of five foot by a wee bit. Why say a wee bit when she might have said ‘a little bit,’ like everybody else? She wanted to make it touching, a proper peasant feeling. Can a Russian peasant be said to feel anything, next to an educated man? In his ignorance he can’t be said to have any feeling at all. Since I was a child, whenever I hear ‘a wee bit,’ I nearly burst with rage. I hate all Russia, Marya Kondratyevna.”

old: “Yet he called me a stinking lackey. He thinks I might turn unruly. There he’s mistaken. If I had a certain sum in my pocket, I’d have left here long ago. Dmitri Fyodorovitch is lower than any lackey in how he behaves, how he thinks and how poor he is. He can’t do anything, and still everyone respects him. I may be only a soup-maker, but with a bit of luck I could open a café restaurant in Petrovka, in Moscow, because my cooking is something special, and in Moscow nobody’s cooking is special except the foreigners’. Dmitri Fyodorovitch is a beggar, but if he challenged the son of the first count in the land, the count would fight him. And yet how is he better than I am? He’s ever so much stupider than I am. Look at all the money he’s thrown away for no reason!”

old: “On the contrary, it’s a coincidence that startles me,” cried Ivan, warmly and good-humoredly. “Believe it or not, ever since that scene with her I’ve been thinking of nothing but my youthful greenness, and then you start in on exactly that, as if you’d guessed. Do you know what I’ve been telling myself, sitting here? Say I didn’t believe in life. Say I’d lost faith in the woman I love and in the order of things, and was convinced that it’s all a disorderly, damnable, maybe devil-ridden chaos. Say I’d been hit by every horror of human disillusionment. I would still want to live. Once I’d tasted the cup, I wouldn’t turn away until I’d drained it! At thirty, though, I’m sure to put the cup down, even half full, and turn away—to where, I don’t know. But until thirty I know my youth will win out over everything, every disillusionment, every disgust with life. Many times I’ve asked myself whether any despair exists that could beat this frantic and perhaps indecent thirst for life in me. I’ve decided that none does—until I’m thirty, that is; after that it will leave me by itself, I imagine. Some drivelling, consumptive moralists, poets especially, often call that thirst for life low. It is a Karamazov trait, true enough, this thirst for life whatever happens. You have it too, no doubt. But why is it low? The centripetal force on our planet is still fearfully strong, Alyosha. I long for life, and I keep on living in spite of logic. I may not believe in the order of the universe, yet I love the sticky little leaves when they open in spring. I love the blue sky. I love certain people, whom one loves, you know, sometimes without knowing why. I love certain great deeds done by men, though I lost faith in them long ago, perhaps; but from old habit the heart still treasures them. Here, they’ve brought your soup. Eat it, it’ll do you good. It’s first-rate soup, they know how to make it here. I want to travel in Europe, Alyosha, and I’ll leave from here. And yet I know I’m going only to a graveyard—but what a precious graveyard! The dead who lie there are precious. Every stone over them tells of such burning life in the past, such passionate faith in their work, their truth, their struggle, their science, that I know I’ll fall to the ground, kiss those stones and weep over them. Though I’m convinced in my heart that it’s long been nothing but a graveyard. And I won’t weep out of despair. I’ll weep simply because my tears will make me happy; I’ll soak my soul in the feeling. I love the sticky leaves in spring, the blue sky—that’s all there is to it. It has nothing to do with intellect or logic. It’s loving with your insides, with your stomach. You love the first strength of your youth. Do you understand any of my tirade, Alyosha?” Ivan laughed suddenly.
new: “On the contrary, it’s a coincidence that startles me,” cried Ivan, warmly and good-humoredly. “Believe it or not, ever since that scene with her I’ve been thinking of nothing but my youthful greenness, and then you start in on exactly that, as if you’d guessed. Do you know what I’ve been telling myself, sitting here? Say I didn’t believe in life. Say I’d lost faith in the woman I love and in the order of things, and was convinced that it’s all a disorderly, damnable, maybe devil-ridden chaos. Say I’d been hit by every horror of human disillusionment. I would still want to live. Once I’d tasted the cup, I wouldn’t turn away until I’d drained it! At thirty, though, I’m sure to put the cup down, even if I haven’t emptied it, and turn away—to where, I don’t know. But until thirty I know my youth will win out over everything, every disillusionment, every disgust with life. Many times I’ve asked myself whether any despair exists that could beat this frantic and perhaps unseemly thirst for life in me. I’ve decided that none does—until I’m thirty, that is; after that it will leave me by itself, I imagine. Some driveling, consumptive moralists, poets especially, often call that thirst for life low. It is a Karamazov trait, true enough, this thirst for life whatever happens. You have it too, no doubt. But why is it low? The centripetal force on our planet is still fearfully strong, Alyosha. I long for life, and I keep on living in spite of logic. I may not believe in the order of the universe, yet I love the sticky little leaves when they open in spring. I love the blue sky. I love certain people, whom one loves, you know, sometimes without knowing why. I love certain great deeds done by men, though I lost faith in them long ago, perhaps; but from old habit the heart still treasures them. Here, they’ve brought your soup. Eat it, it’ll do you good. It’s first-rate soup, they know how to make it here. I want to travel in Europe, Alyosha, and I’ll leave from here. And yet I know I’m going only to a graveyard—but what a precious graveyard! The dead who lie there are precious. Every stone over them tells of such burning life in the past, such passionate faith in their work, their truth, their struggle, their science, that I know I’ll fall to the ground, kiss those stones and weep over them. Though I’m convinced in my heart that it’s long been nothing but a graveyard. And I won’t weep out of despair. I’ll weep simply because my tears will make me happy; I’ll soak my soul in the feeling. I love the sticky leaves in spring, the blue sky—that’s all there is to it. It has nothing to do with intellect or logic. It’s loving with your insides, with your stomach. You love the first strength of your youth. Do you understand any of my tirade, Alyosha?” Ivan laughed suddenly.

old: “Oh, by the way,” Ivan went on, as though he hadn’t heard his brother, “I met a Bulgarian in Moscow recently. He told me about the atrocities the Turks and Circassians are committing all over Bulgaria. They’re afraid of a general uprising of the Slavs. They burn villages, kill, rape women and children. They nail prisoners to fences by the ears and leave them there until morning, and in the morning they hang them. All sorts of things you can’t imagine. We sometimes speak of bestial cruelty, but that’s a great injustice and an insult to the beasts. No beast can ever be as cruel as a man, so artistically cruel. A tiger only tears and gnaws. That’s all he can do. It would never occur to him to nail people up by the ears, even if he could. These Turks enjoyed torturing children, too. They cut unborn babies out of their mothers’ wombs. They tossed infants into the air and caught them on their bayonets in front of their mothers. Doing it in front of the mothers was what gave the sport its zest. Here is another scene I found very interesting. Picture a trembling mother holding her baby, with a ring of Turks around her. They’ve thought up an entertainment. They fuss over the baby and laugh to make it laugh. It works, and the baby laughs. At that moment a Turk aims a pistol four inches from the baby’s face. The baby laughs with delight and reaches out its little hands for the pistol. And he pulls the trigger in the baby’s face and blows out its brains. Artistic, isn’t it? Turks are especially fond of sweets, they say, by the way.”

old: “Then he did the same with God,” said Alyosha.
new: “Just as he did with God, then?” said Alyosha.

old: “Those cultivated parents put this poor five-year-old through every torture imaginable. They beat her, thrashed her, kicked her for no reason, until her whole body was one bruise. Then they got more refined in their cruelty. They locked her up all night in an outhouse, in the cold and frost, because she hadn’t asked to be taken out in the night (as if a five-year-old, sleeping her sound, angelic sleep, could be trained to wake and ask!). For that they smeared her face with filth and stuffed it into her mouth, and it was her mother, her own mother, who did this. And that mother could sleep while she heard the poor child groaning! Can you understand why a little creature, who can’t even grasp what is being done to her, should beat her aching little chest with her tiny fist in the dark and the cold, and weep her meek, unresentful tears to ‘dear, kind God’ to protect her? Do you understand that, my friend and brother, you pious, humble novice? Do you understand why this infamy has to exist and is allowed to? I’m told that without it man couldn’t have lived on earth, since he wouldn’t have known good and evil. Why should he know that diabolical good and evil, when it costs so much? The whole world of knowledge isn’t worth that child’s prayer to ‘dear, kind God’! I say nothing about the suffering of grown-up people. They ate the apple, damn them, and the devil take them all! But these little ones! I’m making you suffer, Alyosha. You’re not yourself. I’ll stop if you like.”

old: “One more picture, just one, because it’s so curious and so typical. I only just read it in some collection of Russian antiquities, and I’ve forgotten the name. I’ll have to look it up. It happened in the darkest days of serfdom, early in the century, and long live the Liberator of the People! In those days there was a general with aristocratic connections who owned great estates. He was one of those men (somewhat exceptional even then, I believe) who retire from the service convinced that it has earned them absolute power over the lives of their subjects. There were such men then. So this general settled on his estate of two thousand souls and lived in grand style, lording it over his poor neighbors as if they were hangers-on and jesters. He had kennels with hundreds of hounds and nearly a hundred dog-boys, all in uniform and all mounted. One day a serf-boy, a little child of eight, threw a stone in play and hurt the paw of the general’s favorite hound. ‘Why is my favorite dog lame?’ He is told that the boy threw a stone and hurt its paw. ‘So you did it.’ The general looked the child up and down. ‘Take him.’ They took him. They took him from his mother and kept him locked up all night. Early the next morning the general rides out in full hunting parade, with his hounds, his dependents, dog-boys and huntsmen, all mounted around him. The house servants are summoned to be edified, and in front of them all stands the child’s mother. The child is brought out of the lock-up. It’s a gloomy, cold, foggy autumn day, a capital day for hunting. The general orders the child undressed. The boy is stripped naked. He shivers, numb with terror, not daring to make a sound.... ‘Make him run,’ commands the general. ‘Run! Run!’ shout the dog-boys. The boy runs.... ‘At him!’ yells the general, and he looses the whole pack on the child. The hounds seize him and tear him to pieces before his mother’s eyes!... I believe the general was later declared unfit to run his estates. Well, what did he deserve? To be shot? To be shot, to satisfy our moral feelings? Speak, Alyosha!”

old: “Listen! I took up the case of children only to make my point clearer. As for the other tears of humanity, which soak the earth from its crust to its core, I’ll say nothing about them. I’ve narrowed my subject on purpose. I’m a bug, and I admit in all humility that I can’t understand why the world is arranged the way it is. Men are to blame themselves, I suppose. They were given paradise, they wanted freedom, and they stole fire from heaven, knowing they would be made unhappy. So there’s no need to pity them. All I know, with my pitiful, earthly, Euclidian mind, is that there is suffering and nobody is guilty; that cause follows effect plainly and directly; that everything flows and finds its level. But that’s only Euclidian nonsense, I know it, and I can’t agree to live by it! What comfort is it to me that nobody is guilty, that cause follows effect plainly and directly, and that I know it? I must have justice, or I’ll destroy myself. And not justice in some remote, infinite time and place, but here on earth, where I can see it myself. I have believed in it. I want to see it, and if I’m dead by then, let me rise again. If it all happens without me, that will be too unfair. Surely I didn’t suffer just so that my crimes and my sufferings could manure the ground for somebody else’s future harmony. I want to see with my own eyes the hind lie down with the lion, and the victim rise up and embrace his murderer. I want to be there when everyone suddenly understands what it was all for. Every religion in the world is built on this longing, and I am a believer. But then there are the children, and what am I to do about them? That’s the question I can’t answer. For the hundredth time I say it: there are masses of questions, but I’ve taken only the children, because in their case what I mean is unanswerably clear. Listen! If everyone has to suffer in order to pay for the eternal harmony, what do children have to do with it? Tell me, please. It’s beyond all understanding why they should suffer, and why they should have to pay for the harmony. Why should they, too, be material to enrich the soil for somebody’s future harmony? I understand solidarity among men in sin. I understand solidarity in retribution, too. But there can be no such solidarity with children. And if it’s really true that they share the responsibility for all their fathers’ crimes, then that truth does not belong to this world, and I can’t comprehend it. Some jester will say that the child would have grown up and sinned. But he didn’t grow up, you see. He was torn to pieces by dogs at eight years old. Oh, Alyosha, I’m not blaspheming! I do understand what an upheaval of the universe it will be, when everything in heaven and on earth blends into one hymn of praise, and everything that lives and has lived cries aloud: ‘You are just, O Lord, for Your ways are revealed.’ When the mother embraces the fiend who threw her child to the dogs, and all three cry aloud through their tears, ‘You are just, O Lord!’ then, of course, the crown of knowledge will have been reached and everything will be clear. But this is exactly where I stop: I can’t accept that harmony. And while I’m still on earth, I make haste to take my own measures. You see, Alyosha, it may really happen that if I live to see that moment, or rise again to witness it, I too will cry out with the rest, as I watch the mother embrace her child’s torturer, ‘You are just, O Lord!’ But I don’t want to cry it out then. While there’s still time, I hurry to protect myself, and so I turn down the higher harmony altogether. It isn’t worth the tears of that one tortured child, who beat her little chest with her little fist and prayed in her stinking outhouse, with her unatoned tears, to ‘dear, kind God’! It isn’t worth it, because those tears were never atoned for. They have to be atoned for, or there can be no harmony. But how? How will you atone for them? Is it even possible? By avenging them? But what do I care about avenging them? What do I care about a hell for the oppressors? What good can hell do, when those children have already been tortured? And what becomes of harmony, if there is a hell? I want to forgive. I want to embrace. I don’t want any more suffering. And if the suffering of children goes to make up the sum of suffering needed to pay for the truth, then I protest that the truth isn’t worth such a price. I don’t want the mother to embrace the oppressor who had her son thrown to the dogs! She has no right to forgive him! Let her forgive him for herself, if she wants to. Let her forgive the torturer for the immeasurable suffering of her own mother’s heart. But the suffering of her tortured child she has no right to forgive. She can’t forgive the torturer, even if the child forgave him! And if that’s so, if they have no right to forgive, what becomes of harmony? Is there anyone in the whole world who would have the right to forgive, and could? I don’t want harmony. Out of love for humanity I don’t want it. I’d rather keep my unavenged suffering. I’d rather stay with my unavenged suffering and my unsatisfied indignation, _even if I were wrong_. Besides, the price of harmony is too high. It’s beyond our means to pay so much to get in. And so I hurry to hand back my entrance ticket, and if I’m an honest man, I’m bound to hand it back as soon as I can. That’s what I’m doing. It isn’t God I don’t accept, Alyosha. I just most respectfully return Him the ticket.”

old: “Rebellion? I’m sorry you call it that,” said Ivan earnestly. “Nobody can live in rebellion for long, and I want to live. Tell me yourself, I challenge you, answer. Suppose you were building the fabric of human destiny, with the aim of making people happy in the end and giving them peace and rest at last. But suppose it was essential and unavoidable to torture to death just one tiny creature, that baby beating her chest with her fist, for example, and to build that edifice on her unavenged tears. Would you agree to be the architect on those terms? Tell me, and tell the truth.”

But there is a Being, and He can forgive everything, all and for all, because He gave His innocent blood for all and for everything. You’ve forgotten Him, and the edifice is built on Him, and it is to Him they cry aloud, ‘You are just, O Lord, for Your ways are revealed!’”

old: “Not a bit of it! He claims it as a merit for himself and his Church that they have at last conquered freedom, and done it to make men happy. ‘For now’ (he means the Inquisition, of course) ‘for the first time, it has become possible to think about men’s happiness. Man was made a rebel, and how can rebels be happy? You were warned,’ he tells Him. ‘You had plenty of admonitions and warnings, but You did not heed them. You rejected the one way by which men could be made happy. But luckily, when You left, You passed the work on to us. You promised it, You confirmed it by Your word, You gave us the right to bind and to unbind. So of course You cannot now think of taking it away. Why, then, have You come to stand in our way?’”

old: “‘That is what the first question in the wilderness meant. That is what You turned down, for the sake of the freedom You placed above everything else. Yet the great secret of this world lies hidden in that question. Had You chosen “bread,” You would have met the one need all humanity has, always—the need to find someone to worship. A man who is free has no goal he pursues so restlessly and so painfully as this: to find someone to worship. But he wants to worship something no one can dispute, something so plainly established that all men would agree at once to bow to it. These pitiful creatures are not satisfied to find what this man or that man can worship. They must find something that everyone will believe in and worship, and above all they must do it _together_. This craving for worship in _common_ has been the chief misery of each man, and of the whole race, since time began. For the sake of common worship they have put each other to the sword. They have set up gods and challenged one another: “Put away your gods and come and worship ours, or we will kill you and your gods!” So it will be until the end of the world, even when the gods have vanished from the earth. They will fall down before idols all the same. You knew this basic secret of human nature. You could not help knowing it. Yet You refused the one sure banner that was held out to You, the banner that would have made every man bow down to You alone—the banner of earthly bread. You refused it for the sake of freedom and the bread of Heaven. Now see what You did next. And again, all of it in the name of freedom! I tell You, no anxiety torments man more than the need to find, and quickly, someone to whom he can hand over the gift of freedom with which the poor creature is born. But only one who can quiet their conscience can take their freedom from them. In bread You were offered a banner nothing could beat: give men bread and they will worship You, because nothing is more certain than bread. But if someone else gets hold of man’s conscience—oh! then he will throw away Your bread and follow the one who has trapped his conscience. In that You were right. The secret of man’s existence is not just to live, but to have something to live for. Without a firm idea of what he lives for, man would not agree to go on living. He would rather destroy himself than stay on earth, even with bread in plenty. That is true. But what came of it? Instead of taking men’s freedom away, You made it greater than ever! Did You forget that man prefers peace, even death, to the freedom of choosing in the knowledge of good and evil? Nothing tempts man more than his freedom of conscience, and nothing makes him suffer more. And now see: instead of building a firm foundation to put man’s conscience at rest for ever, You chose everything that is exceptional, vague and puzzling. You chose what was wholly beyond men’s strength, and acted as though You did not love them at all—You, who came to give Your life for them! Instead of taking over men’s freedom, You added to it. You loaded the spiritual kingdom of mankind with its sufferings for ever. You wanted man’s love given freely. You wanted him to follow You freely, drawn and made captive by You. In place of the rigid ancient law, man would now have to decide for himself, with a free heart, what is good and what is evil, with only Your image before him as a guide. But did You not know that in the end he would reject even Your image and Your truth, once the fearful burden of free choice weighed him down? In the end they will cry out that the truth is not in You.
