new: “‘That is what the first question in the wilderness meant. That is what You turned down, for the sake of the freedom You placed above everything else. Yet the great secret of this world lies hidden in that question. Had You chosen “bread,” You would have satisfied the universal and everlasting craving of all humanity—the craving to find someone to worship. A man who is free has no goal he pursues so restlessly and so painfully as this: to find someone to worship. But he wants to worship something no one can dispute, something so plainly established that all men would agree at once to bow to it. These pitiful creatures are not satisfied to find what this man or that man can worship. They must find something that everyone will believe in and worship, and above all they must do it _together_. This craving for worship in _common_ has been the chief misery of each man, and of the whole race, since time began. For the sake of common worship they have put each other to the sword. They have set up gods and challenged one another: “Put away your gods and come and worship ours, or we will kill you and your gods!” So it will be until the end of the world, even when the gods have vanished from the earth. They will fall down before idols all the same. You knew this basic secret of human nature. You could not help knowing it. Yet You refused the one sure banner that was held out to You, the banner that would have made every man bow down to You alone—the banner of earthly bread. You refused it for the sake of freedom and the bread of Heaven. Now see what You did next. And again, all of it in the name of freedom! I tell You, no anxiety torments man more than the need to find, and quickly, someone to whom he can hand over the gift of freedom with which the poor creature is born. But only one who can quiet their conscience can take their freedom from them. In bread You were offered a banner nothing could beat: give men bread and they will worship You, because nothing is more certain than bread. But if someone else gets hold of man’s conscience—oh! then he will throw away Your bread and follow the one who has trapped his conscience. In that You were right. The secret of man’s existence is not just to live, but to have something to live for. Without a firm idea of what he lives for, man would not agree to go on living. He would rather destroy himself than stay on earth, even with bread in plenty. That is true. But what came of it? Instead of taking men’s freedom away, You made it greater than ever! Did You forget that man prefers peace, even death, to the freedom of choosing in the knowledge of good and evil? Nothing tempts man more than his freedom of conscience, and nothing makes him suffer more. And now see: instead of building a firm foundation to put man’s conscience at rest for ever, You chose everything that is exceptional, vague and puzzling. You chose what was wholly beyond men’s strength, and acted as though You did not love them at all—You, who came to give Your life for them! Instead of taking over men’s freedom, You added to it. You loaded the spiritual kingdom of mankind with its sufferings for ever. You wanted man’s love given freely. You wanted him to follow You freely, drawn and made captive by You. In place of the rigid ancient law, man would now have to decide for himself, with a free heart, what is good and what is evil, with only Your image before him as a guide. But did You not know that in the end he would reject even Your image and Your truth, once the fearful burden of free choice weighed him down? In the end they will cry out that the truth is not in You. They could not have been left in worse confusion and torment than You have left them in, piling on them so many cares and so many problems that have no answer.

old: “‘When they receive bread from us, they will see plainly that we take the bread their own hands have made, only to hand it back to them, and that there is no miracle in it. They will see that we do not turn stones into bread. Yet in truth they will be more grateful for receiving it from our hands than for the bread itself! They will remember only too well that in the old days, without our help, even the bread they made turned to stones in their hands, while since they came back to us, the very stones have turned to bread in their hands. Far too well will they understand the value of complete submission! And until men understand that, they will be unhappy. Who is most to blame that they do not? Speak! Who scattered the flock and sent it wandering down unknown paths? But the flock will gather again and submit once more, and this time it will be for good. Then we shall give them the quiet, humble happiness of weak creatures, which is what they are by nature. Oh, we shall persuade them in the end not to be proud, because You lifted them up and so taught them pride. We shall show them that they are weak, that they are nothing but pitiful children, and that a child’s happiness is the sweetest there is. They will grow timid. They will look to us and press close to us in fear, as chicks do to the hen. They will marvel at us and stand in awe of us. They will take pride in our being so powerful and so clever that we could tame a flock this unruly, thousands of millions strong. They will tremble helplessly when we are angry, their minds will fill with fear, and they will cry as easily as women and children do. But at a sign from us they will turn just as readily to laughter and rejoicing, to happy mirth and childish song. Yes, we shall make them work, but in their free hours we shall arrange their life like a child’s game, with children’s songs and innocent dances. Oh, we shall even let them sin. They are weak and helpless, and they will love us like children because we let them sin. We shall tell them that every sin will be atoned for if it is done with our permission. We let them sin because we love them, we shall say, and the punishment for these sins we take on ourselves. And we shall take it on ourselves, and they will adore us as the saviors who have borne their sins before God. They will keep no secrets from us. We shall permit or forbid them to live with their wives and mistresses, and to have children or not, depending on whether they have obeyed or disobeyed, and they will submit to us gladly and cheerfully. The most painful secrets of their conscience, every one of them, they will bring to us, and we shall have an answer for all. They will be glad to believe our answer, for it will spare them the great anxiety and the terrible agony they suffer now, having to decide freely for themselves. And all will be happy, all the millions of creatures, except the hundred thousand who rule over them. For only we, who guard the mystery, will be unhappy. There will be thousands of millions of happy babes, and a hundred thousand sufferers who have taken on themselves the curse of the knowledge of good and evil. Peacefully they will die, peacefully they will expire in Your name, and beyond the grave they will find nothing but death. But we shall keep the secret, and for their happiness we shall tempt them on with the reward of heaven and eternity. Though if there were anything in the other world, it certainly would not be for such as they. It is prophesied that You will come again in victory, with Your chosen, the proud and the strong. But we will say that they have saved only themselves, and we have saved everyone. We are told that the harlot who sits upon the beast, holding the _mystery_ in her hands, will be put to shame; that the weak will rise up again, tear her royal purple, and strip her loathsome body bare. But then I will stand up and show You the thousand millions of happy children who have never known sin. And we, who took their sins on ourselves for their happiness, will stand before You and say: “Judge us, if You can and dare.” Know that I do not fear You. Know that I too have been in the wilderness, that I too lived on roots and locusts, that I too prized the freedom You have blessed men with, and that I too was struggling to take my place among Your elect, among the strong and mighty, hungering “to make up the number.” But I woke up, and I refused to serve madness. I turned back and joined the ranks of those _who have corrected Your work_. I left the proud and returned to the humble, for the humble’s happiness. What I tell You will come to pass, and our dominion will be built. I repeat, tomorrow You will see that obedient flock, which at one sign from me will rush to pile the glowing coals around the stake where I shall burn You for coming to hinder us. For if anyone has ever deserved our fires, it is You. Tomorrow I shall burn You. _Dixi._’”

old: “So what if it is! You’ve finally guessed it. It’s perfectly true, that is the whole secret. But isn’t that suffering, at least for a man like him, who has thrown away his whole life in the desert and still could not shake off his incurable love for humanity? In his old age he arrived at a clear conviction: only the advice of the great, dread spirit could make any tolerable life for those feeble, unruly ‘incomplete, experimental creatures made as a joke.’ Convinced of this, he sees that he has to follow the counsel of the wise spirit, the dread spirit of death and destruction. So he has to accept lies and deception, and lead men knowingly to death and destruction, while deceiving them the whole way so that they never notice where they are being taken. That way the poor blind creatures can at least believe themselves happy on the road. And mark this: the deception is carried out in the name of Him whose ideal the old man believed in so fervently all his life. Isn’t that tragic? And if just one such man stood at the head of the whole army ‘filled with the lust for power only for the sake of filthy gain,’ wouldn’t one be enough to make a tragedy? More than that, one such man at the head is enough to produce the true guiding idea of the Roman Church, with all its armies and Jesuits, its highest idea. I tell you frankly, I firmly believe there has always been a man like that among those at the head of the movement. Who knows, there may have been some even among the Roman Popes. Who knows, perhaps the spirit of that accursed old man, who loves mankind so obstinately in his own fashion, lives on right now in a whole crowd of such old men. They would exist not by chance but by agreement, as a secret league formed long ago to guard the mystery, to guard it from the weak and unhappy, in order to make them happy. No doubt that’s how it is, and how it has to be. I suspect even the Masons have something of the same mystery at bottom, and that’s why the Catholics hate the Masons so, as rivals who break up the unity of the idea, when it is so essential that there be one flock and one shepherd.... But the way I’m defending my idea, I might be an author who can’t take your criticism. Enough of that.”

old: “This is how I meant to end it. When the Inquisitor finished speaking, he waited a while for his Prisoner to answer. The silence was heavy on him. He had seen that the Prisoner listened closely the whole time, gazing gently into his face, and clearly did not want to reply. The old man longed for Him to say something, however bitter and terrible. Instead He came up to the old man without a word and kissed him softly on his bloodless, aged lips. That was His whole answer. The old man shuddered. His lips twitched. He went to the door, opened it, and said to Him: ‘Go, and come no more... do not come at all, never, never!’ And he let Him out into the dark streets of the town. The Prisoner went away.”

old: “Oh, it’s all nonsense, Alyosha. It’s just a senseless poem by a senseless student who never managed to write two lines of verse. Why take it so seriously? You can’t think I’m about to run off to the Jesuits and join the men who are correcting His work? Good Lord, that’s none of my business. I told you, all I want is to hold out until thirty, and then... dash the cup to the ground!”

old: Ivan left Alyosha and walked home to Fyodor Pavlovitch’s house. But oddly, a crushing gloom settled on him, and it grew heavier with every step he took toward the house. Being gloomy was nothing odd. What was odd was that Ivan could not say why. He had been low before. And it was hardly surprising that he felt low now, when he had cut every tie that had brought him here and was about to start afresh, that very day, on a new and unknown future. He would be as lonely as ever. He had great hopes, and great—too great—expectations of life, but he could not have said clearly what his hopes were, or his expectations, or even what he wanted.

old: “Blast it! What makes you so certain you’re going to have a fit, damn you? Are you laughing at me?”
new: “Blast it! What makes you so certain you’re going to have a fit, confound you? Are you laughing at me?”

old: “Damn it! If you’re laid up, Grigory will be keeping watch. Tell Grigory ahead of time, and he’ll certainly keep him out.”
new: “Confound it! If you’re laid up, Grigory will be keeping watch. Tell Grigory ahead of time, and he’ll certainly keep him out.”

old: “And why would he go to father at all, least of all sneaking in, if Agrafena Alexandrovna isn’t coming, as you say yourself?” Ivan went on, going white with anger. “You say so yourself, and the whole time I’ve been here I’ve been sure it was all the old man’s delusion and that the creature won’t come to him. Why would Dmitri burst in on him if she doesn’t come? Speak up, I want to know what you’re thinking!”

old: “Nonsense!” cried Ivan, nearly beside himself. “Dmitri won’t come to rob anyone, or to kill my father for the money. He might have killed him yesterday over Grushenka, the frantic, savage fool, but he won’t steal.”
new: “Nonsense!” cried Ivan, nearly beside himself. “Dmitri won’t come to steal money and kill my father to get it. He might have killed him yesterday over Grushenka, the frantic, savage fool, but he won’t steal.”

old: The old man was absolutely delighted. He wrote the note and sent for the horses. A light lunch was brought in, with brandy. When Fyodor Pavlovitch was pleased, he usually became expansive, but today he seemed to hold himself back. He did not say a word about Dmitri, for instance. The parting left him quite unmoved, and he actually seemed at a loss for something to say. Ivan noticed this particularly. “He must be sick of me,” he thought. Only when he went out with his son onto the steps did the old man start to fuss. He would have kissed him, but Ivan hurried to hold out his hand, plainly avoiding the kiss. His father saw it at once and immediately pulled himself up.

old: “Father and teacher,” he began, deeply moved, “your words are too dark to me.... What is this suffering that awaits him?”
new: “Father and teacher,” he began, deeply moved, “your words are too obscure.... What is this suffering that awaits him?”

old: “Do not ask. Yesterday I seemed to see something terrible ... as if his whole future were written in his eyes. There came a look into his eyes—and I was struck with horror at once, at what that man is preparing for himself. Once or twice in my life I have seen that look on a man’s face ... showing, as it were, the fate in store for him, and that fate, alas, came to pass. I sent you to him, Alexey, because I thought the sight of a brother’s face would help him. But everything, and all our fates, come from the Lord. ‘Except a corn of wheat fall into the ground and die, it abideth alone; but if it die, it bringeth forth much fruit.’ Remember that. As for you, Alexey, many times I have blessed you silently because of your face. Know that,” added the elder, with a gentle smile. “This is what I think of you. You will leave these walls, but you will live in the world like a monk. You will have many enemies, yet even your enemies will love you. Life will bring you many misfortunes, but in them you will find your happiness, and you will bless life and make others bless it, which is what matters most. Well, that is your character. Fathers and teachers,” he said to his friends with a tender smile, “until today I have never told even him why this young man’s face is so dear to me. Now I will tell you. His face has been for me a remembrance and a prophecy together. When I was a child, at the dawn of my life, I had an elder brother who died before my eyes at the age of seventeen. As my life went on, I gradually came to believe that this brother was meant as a guide and a sign from above for me. Had he not entered my life, I should never have become a monk and set foot on this precious path, or so I think. He appeared to me first in my childhood, and now, at the end of my pilgrimage, it seems he has come to me a second time. It is marvelous, fathers and teachers. Alexey bears some resemblance to him in face, though not a great one. But in spirit he seems to me so like him that many times I have taken him for that young man, my brother, come back to me mysteriously at the end of my journey to remind and inspire me. I was truly amazed at so strange a fancy in myself. Do you hear this, Porfiry?” He turned to the novice who attended him. “Many times I have seen a look of hurt in your face, because I love Alexey more than you. Now you know the reason. But I love you too, know that, and many times I was grieved by your hurt. Dear friends, I want to tell you about that youth, my brother, for no one who has been in my life was more precious, more full of meaning, or more touching. My heart is full of tenderness, and at this moment I look at my whole life as though I were living it over again.”

old: Beloved fathers and teachers, I was born in a remote northern province, in the town of V. My father was a gentleman by birth, but he had no great standing or rank. He died when I was two years old, and I have no memory of him at all. He left my mother a small house built of wood and a modest fortune, but enough to keep her and her children comfortably. There were two of us, my elder brother Markel and I. He was eight years older than I was. He had a hasty, irritable temper, but he was kind-hearted and never sneering. He was remarkably silent, especially at home, with me, with his mother and with the servants. He did well at school but could not get along with his schoolmates, though he never fought with them, or so my mother has told me. Six months before his death, when he was seventeen, he became friends with a political exile. This man had been sent from Moscow to our town for freethinking, and he lived there alone. He was a fine scholar who had distinguished himself in philosophy at the university. Something drew him to Markel, and he often asked him to visit. That winter the young man spent whole evenings with him, until the exile was called to Petersburg to take up his post again, at his own request, since he had powerful friends.

He did well at school but could not get along with his schoolmates, though he never quarreled with them, or so my mother has told me. Six months before his death, when he was seventeen, he became friends with a political exile. This man had been sent from Moscow to our town for freethinking, and he lived there alone. He was a fine scholar who had distinguished himself in philosophy at the university. Something drew him to Markel, and he often asked him to visit. That winter the young man spent whole evenings with him, until the exile was called to Petersburg to take up his post again, at his own request, since he had powerful friends.

old: From the house of my childhood I have brought away nothing but precious memories. No memories are more precious than those of early childhood in one’s first home, and that is almost always so, as long as there is any love and harmony in the family at all. Even a bad home can leave precious memories, if only the heart knows how to find what is precious in it. Among my memories of home I count my memories of the Bible, which I was very eager to read as a child. I had a book of Scripture history then, with excellent pictures, called _A Hundred and Four Stories from the Old and New Testament_. I learned to read from it. It lies on my shelf now, and I keep it as a precious relic of the past. But even before I could read, I was moved to devotion for the first time, at eight years old. I remember it well. My mother took me alone to the service on the Monday before Easter. (I do not remember where my brother was.) The day was fine. I remember it today as though I saw it now: the incense rose from the censer and floated softly upwards, and up in the cupola it mingled, in rising waves, with the sunlight streaming through the little window. The sight stirred me, and for the first time in my life I consciously received the seed of God’s word in my heart. A youth came out into the middle of the church carrying a big book. It was so large that I thought he could scarcely carry it. He laid it on the reading desk and opened it and began to read, and suddenly, for the first time, I understood something that was read in the church of God. In the land of Uz there lived a man, righteous and God-fearing, who had great wealth: so many camels, so many sheep and asses. His children feasted, and he loved them dearly and prayed for them. “It may be that my sons have sinned in their feasting.” Then the devil came before the Lord, together with the sons of God, and told the Lord that he had gone up and down the earth and under the earth. “And have you considered my servant Job?” God asked him. God boasted to the devil of His great and holy servant, and the devil laughed at God’s words. “Give him over to me, and you will see that Your servant will murmur against You and curse Your name.” So God gave up the just man He loved so much into the devil’s hands. And the devil struck down his children and his cattle and scattered his wealth, all at once, like a thunderbolt from heaven. Job tore his mantle and fell to the ground and cried aloud, “Naked came I out of my mother’s womb, and naked shall I return into the earth. The Lord gave and the Lord has taken away. Blessed be the name of the Lord for ever and ever.”

old: When I came back two months later, I found the young lady already married to a rich landowner of the neighborhood. He was a very amiable man, still young though older than I was, connected with the best Petersburg society, which I was not, and well educated, which I also was not. I was so overwhelmed by this unexpected blow that my mind was positively clouded. The worst of it was that, as I learned then, the young landowner had been engaged to her for a long time. I had met him many times in her house, but blinded by my conceit I had noticed nothing. And this mortified me most of all: almost everybody had known about it, while I knew nothing. I was filled with sudden, uncontrollable fury. My face burned as I recalled how often I had been on the point of declaring my love to her. She had not tried to stop me or warn me, so I concluded that she must have been laughing at me all the time. Later, of course, I thought it over and remembered that she had been very far from laughing at me. On the contrary, she used to turn aside any love-making of mine with a joke and start talking about other things. But at that moment I could not reflect, and I was all eagerness for revenge. I am surprised, remembering it, that my rage and vengefulness were so foreign to my own nature. I was easygoing and found it hard to stay angry with anyone for long. So I had to work myself up artificially, and I ended by becoming revolting and absurd.

old: I was in ecstasy, laughing and chattering all the way. I don’t remember about what.
new: I was in ecstasy, laughing and chattering all the way. I do not remember about what.

old: The seconds were shouting too, mine most of all: “To face your opponent and beg his pardon, and disgrace the regiment like this! If I had only known!”
new: The seconds were shouting too, mine most of all: “Can you disgrace the regiment like this, facing your opponent and begging his pardon! If I had only known!”

old: I enjoyed listening to them and looking at them. “My dear friends and comrades,” said I, “do not trouble yourselves about my resigning, because I have already done it. I sent in my papers this morning, and as soon as I get my discharge I shall enter a monastery. That is why I am leaving the regiment.”

old: It was the same with the society of the town. Until then I had been received kindly but had attracted no special attention. Now everyone got to know me at once, and everyone invited me. They laughed at me, but they loved me. I should mention that although everybody talked openly about our duel, the authorities paid it no mind. My antagonist was a close relation of our general, and since no blood had been shed and nothing serious had come of it, and since I had resigned my commission, they treated it as a joke. And from then on I began to speak out loud and without fear, whatever they laughed at, for their laughter was always kindly and never spiteful. These conversations mostly took place in the evenings, in the company of ladies. Women especially liked to hear me, and they made the men listen.

old: “I ... you know ... I killed someone.”
new: “I ... you know ... I murdered someone.”

old: “So you do not believe it?” he said. “You preach it and do not believe it yourself. Believe me, this dream, as you call it, will certainly come true. It will come, but not yet, for every process has its law. This is a spiritual, a psychological process. If the world is to be changed and made new, men must first turn to another path in their minds. Until you have truly become a brother to everyone, brotherhood will not come. No science, no common interest, will ever teach men to share property and privilege with the same fairness to all. Everyone will think his share too small. They will always be envying one another, complaining and attacking. You ask when it will come. It will come, but first we must pass through a time of isolation.”

old: For a long time I could not believe him. I did not believe him then, only after he had come to me three days running and told me all of it. I thought he was mad, but I ended by being convinced, to my great grief and amazement. His crime was great and terrible.

old: “Good Lord!” I thought. “At a moment like this he is thinking about what other people will respect!” I felt so sorry for him that I believe I would have shared his fate if that could have comforted him. I saw he was beside himself. I was horrified, for I understood with my heart as well as my mind what such a decision meant.

old: Then he took out all the things he had kept for fourteen years as proof of his crime and laid them on the table. There were the murdered woman’s jewels, which he had stolen to turn suspicion away. There was a cross and a locket taken from her neck, with a portrait of her betrothed inside. There was her notebook, and two letters: one from her betrothed, telling her he would soon be with her, and her unfinished reply, left on the table to be sent next day. He had carried off those two letters—what for? Why had he kept them for fourteen years afterward, instead of destroying them as evidence against him?

old: Fathers and teachers, what is a monk? In the educated world these days, some people say the word with a sneer and others use it as a curse, and this contempt for monks keeps growing. It is true, sadly true, that many monks are sluggards, gluttons, libertines and insolent beggars. Educated people point at these and say: “You are idlers, useless to society. You live off other people’s labor. You are shameless beggars.” Yet there are so many gentle, humble monks who long for solitude and for fervent prayer in peace! People notice them less, or say nothing about them. And how surprised people would be if I told them that the salvation of Russia may come once more from these gentle monks who long to pray alone! For in peace and quiet they are truly being made ready “for the day and the hour, the month and the year.” In the meantime, in their solitude, they keep the image of Christ fair and undefiled, in the purity of God’s truth, just as it came down to them from the Fathers of old, the Apostles and the martyrs. When the time comes, they will show it to the wavering creeds of the world. That is a great thought. That star will rise out of the East.

old: The monastic way is very different. People laugh at obedience, fasting and prayer, yet only through them lies the road to real, true freedom. I cut away my superfluous, unnecessary desires. I subdue my proud and wanton will and discipline it with obedience. With God’s help I reach freedom of spirit, and with it spiritual joy. Who is better able to conceive a great idea and serve it, the rich man in his isolation, or the man who has freed himself from the tyranny of material things and habits? People reproach the monk for his solitude: “You have shut yourself away behind monastery walls to save your own soul, and forgotten the brotherly service of humanity!” But we shall see who proves the more zealous for brotherly love. For it is not we who are isolated but they, though they cannot see it. In the old days the leaders of the people came from among us, and why not again? The same gentle, humble ascetics will rise up and go out to work for the great cause. The salvation of Russia comes from the people, and the Russian monk has always stood with the people. We are isolated only if the people are isolated. The people believe as we do. A reformer who does not believe will never accomplish anything in Russia, however sincere his heart and however great his genius. Remember that! The people will meet the atheist and overcome him, and Russia will be one and Orthodox. Take care of the peasant and guard his heart. Go on educating him quietly. That is your duty as monks, for the peasant has God in his heart.

old: Fathers and teachers, watch over the people’s faith, and this will not be a dream. All my life our great people have struck me with their dignity, a true and seemly dignity. I have seen it with my own eyes and I can bear witness to it. I have seen it and marveled at it, despite the degrading sins and the poverty-stricken look of our peasants. They are not servile. Even after two centuries of serfdom they are free in manner and bearing, without insolence, and neither revengeful nor envious. “You are rich and noble, you are clever and talented. Well, be so, God bless you. I respect you, but I know that I too am a man. By respecting you without envy, I prove my dignity as a man.”

old: And we may put a question to the scornful themselves: if our hope is a dream, when will you build your edifice and order things justly by your intellect alone, without Christ? If they declare that they are the ones advancing toward unity, only the simplest-hearted among them believe it. One can truly marvel at such simplicity. In truth, their dreams are more fantastic than ours. They aim at justice, but they deny Christ, and they will end by flooding the earth with blood, for blood cries out for blood, and he that taketh up the sword shall perish by the sword. Without Christ’s covenant they would slaughter one another down to the last two men on earth. Those last two would be too proud to restrain each other, and one would kill the other and then himself. That would come to pass, were it not for Christ’s promise that for the sake of the humble and meek the days shall be shortened.

old: My friends, ask God for gladness. Be glad like children, like the birds of heaven. And do not let men’s sin trouble you in your work. Do not fear that it will wear your work away and keep it from being finished. Do not say, “Sin is mighty, wickedness is mighty, our evil surroundings are mighty, and we are alone and helpless. Our evil surroundings are wearing us away and keeping our good work from being done.” Flee from that gloom, children! There is only one way to be saved. Take the blame on yourself and make yourself answerable for the sins of all men. That is the truth, you know, friends. As soon as you sincerely make yourself answerable for everything and for everyone, you will see at once that it really is so, and that you are to blame for every person and every thing. But if you push your own laziness and weakness onto others, you will end by sharing the pride of Satan and complaining against God.

old: God took seeds from other worlds and sowed them on this earth. His garden grew, and everything came up that could come up. But whatever grows is alive only through its sense of touching other, mysterious worlds. If that feeling grows weak in you, or is destroyed, the heavenly growth in you will die. Then you will be indifferent to life, and you may even come to hate it. That is what I think.

old: In the end the elder’s death came quite unexpectedly. The people gathered around him that last evening knew that his death was near. Still, it was hard to imagine it would come so suddenly. On the contrary, as I said before, his friends saw him that night so cheerful and talkative that they were convinced his condition had changed for the better, at least for a time. Even five minutes before he died, they said afterwards in amazement, there was no way of foreseeing it. He seemed suddenly to feel a sharp pain in his chest. He went pale and pressed his hands to his heart. Everyone got up from their seats and hurried to him. But though he was in pain, he still looked at them with a smile. He slid slowly from his chair to his knees, then bowed his face to the ground, stretched out his arms, and, as if in joyful ecstasy, praying and kissing the ground, he quietly and joyfully gave up his soul to God.

old: Father Iosif walked away, grieved all the more because he had put his opinion forward so timidly, as if he hardly believed it himself. He could see, to his distress, that something very unseemly was beginning, and that disobedience was plainly on its way. One by one, all the sensible monks were silenced, as Father Iosif had been. The result was that everyone who loved the elder and had accepted the eldership with devout obedience was suddenly crushed, and exchanged timid glances when they met. The enemies of elders, who saw the institution as a novelty, now carried their heads proudly. “The late elder Varsonofy gave off no smell of corruption, but a sweet fragrance,” they reminded everyone, with spite. “But he earned that glory not as an elder, but as a holy man.”

old: “Have you, too, been led into temptation?” cried Father Païssy. “Are you with those of little faith?” he added sadly.
new: “Have you, too, fallen into temptation?” cried Father Païssy. “Can you be with those of little faith?” he added sadly.

old: Father Païssy was right, of course, to decide that his “dear boy” would come back. He may even have seen, to some degree, what Alyosha’s spiritual state really meant. Still, I have to admit that I would find it very hard to give a clear account of that strange, hazy time in the life of the young hero I love so much. Father Païssy asked sadly, “Are you too with those of little faith?” I could answer confidently for Alyosha, “No, he is not with those of little faith. Quite the opposite.” All his trouble, in fact, came from having great faith. But the trouble was there just the same, and it hurt so badly that even long afterwards Alyosha remembered that sorrowful day as one of the bitterest and most fatal of his life. Suppose someone asks: “Can all his grief and turmoil really have come only from the fact that his elder’s body showed signs of early decay, instead of working miracles at once?” I have to answer without beating about the bush, “Yes, it certainly can.” I only ask the reader not to hurry to laugh at my young hero’s pure heart. I have no wish to apologize for him, or to excuse his innocent faith by pointing to his youth, or how little he had studied, or any such thing. On the contrary, I declare that I truly respect the qualities of his heart. A youth who took in impressions cautiously, whose love was lukewarm, and whose mind was too prudent for his age and therefore worth little, might well, I admit, have escaped what happened to my hero. But sometimes it does a man more credit to be swept away by a feeling, however unreasonable, that grows out of great love, than to remain unmoved. This is even truer in youth, because a young man who is always sensible is not to be trusted and is worth little—that’s my opinion!

But sometimes it does a man more credit to be swept away by a feeling, however unreasonable, that grows out of great love, than to remain unmoved. This is even truer in youth, because a young man who is always sensible is not to be trusted and is worth little—that’s my opinion!

old: “Well, well! You surprise me, brother!” Rakitin stared at him in amazement. “Anyway, vodka or sausage, this is a damned fine chance and we mustn’t miss it. Come on.”
new: “Well, well! You surprise me, brother!” Rakitin stared at him in amazement. “Anyway, vodka or sausage, this is a first-rate chance and we mustn’t miss it. Come on.”

old: “I tell you, I’m waiting for news, priceless news, and so I don’t want Mitya at all. And I feel that he didn’t believe I’d stay at Kuzma Kuzmitch’s. He must be lying in ambush now, in the garden behind Fyodor Pavlovitch’s, watching for me. And if he’s there, he won’t come here, which is all the better! But I really did go to Kuzma Kuzmitch’s. Mitya took me there himself. I told him I’d stay till midnight, and I made him promise to come at midnight without fail and take me home. He left, and I sat ten minutes with Kuzma Kuzmitch and came back here. Ugh, I was scared. I ran, so as not to bump into him.”

old: Alyosha said nothing. He sat there afraid to move. He heard her words, “Tell me, and I’ll get off,” but he did not answer. Still, nothing stirred in his heart of what Rakitin, say, watching him spitefully from his corner, might have expected or imagined. His great grief swallowed every feeling that might have been roused. If he had been able to think clearly just then, he would have seen that he was wearing the strongest armor against every lust and temptation. Yet, dazed as he was and crushed by sorrow, he could not help noticing a new and strange feeling in his heart. This woman, this “dreadful” woman, did not frighten him now. He felt none of the fear that used to rise in his soul whenever a thought of any woman crossed his mind. Quite the opposite. This was the woman he had feared more than any other, and she was sitting on his knee with her arms around him. She woke in him a different, unexpected, odd feeling: the keenest, purest interest, with no trace of his old terror. That was what surprised him, though he could not have said why.

old: “Does he know! Of course not. If he knew, there’d be murder. But I’m not afraid of that now, I’m not afraid of his knife. Quiet, Rakitin, don’t remind me of Dmitri Fyodorovitch. He’s bruised my heart. I don’t want to think about that right now. I can think about Alyosha, I can look at Alyosha ... smile at me, dear, cheer up, smile at my silliness, at my happiness.... Ah, he’s smiling, he’s smiling! How kindly he looks at me! And you know, Alyosha, all this time I’ve been thinking you were angry with me about the day before yesterday, about that young lady. I behaved like a cur, that’s the truth.... But it’s good that it happened. It was horrid, but good as well.” Grushenka smiled dreamily, and a faintly cruel line showed in her smile. “Mitya told me she screamed that I ‘ought to be flogged.’ I did insult her terribly. She sent for me, she wanted to win me over, to bribe me with her chocolate.... No, it’s good that it ended like that.” She smiled again. “But I’m still afraid you’re angry with me.”

old: “Typical woman!”
new: “That’s a woman’s way of looking at it!”

old: “How touching and sentimental!” said Rakitin with a sneer. “And she’s sitting on his knee, too! He has something to grieve over, but what’s your excuse? He’s rebelling against his God and ready to eat sausage....”

old: “Well, I’d hate to be in his place,” Rakitin hissed.
new: “Well, I wouldn’t care to be in his shoes,” Rakitin hissed.

old: “Well, you won’t be, Rakitin. You’ll never be in his place. You shall black my shoes, Rakitin. That’s where you belong. You’ll never get a woman like me ... and he won’t either, perhaps ...”
new: “Well, you won’t be, Rakitin. You’ll never be in his shoes. You shall black my shoes, Rakitin. That’s where you belong. You’ll never get a woman like me ... and he won’t either, perhaps ...”

old: “Don’t taunt me about dressing up, Rakitin. You don’t know everything that’s in my heart! If I choose to tear off my finery, I’ll tear it off at once, this minute,” she cried in a ringing voice. “You don’t know what that finery is for, Rakitin! Perhaps I’ll see him and say, ‘Have you ever seen me look like this before?’ He left me a thin, sickly little crybaby of seventeen. I’ll sit beside him, fascinate him and work him up. ‘Do you see what I’m like now?’ I’ll say to him. ‘Well, that’s all you’re getting, my dear sir. There’s many a slip between the cup and the lip!’ That may be what the finery is for, Rakitin.” Grushenka finished with a spiteful laugh. “I’m violent and I hold grudges, Alyosha. I’ll tear off my finery, I’ll destroy my beauty, I’ll scorch my face, slash it with a knife, and turn beggar. If I choose, I won’t go anywhere now to see anyone. If I choose, I’ll send Kuzma back everything he has ever given me, tomorrow, and all his money, and I’ll go out scrubbing floors for the rest of my life. You think I wouldn’t do it, Rakitin? That I wouldn’t dare? I would, I would, I could do it right now, only don’t push me ... and I’ll send him about his business, I’ll snap my fingers in his face, and he’ll never see me again!”

old: “_Jesus said to her, Woman, what do I have to do with you? Mine hour is not yet come._
new: “_Jesus said to her, Woman, what has it to do with you or me? Mine hour is not yet come._

old: “We are rejoicing,” the little, thin old man went on. “We are drinking the new wine, the wine of a new and great gladness. Do you see how many guests there are? Here are the bride and the bridegroom, and here is the wise governor of the feast, tasting the new wine. Why are you surprised to see me? I gave an onion to a beggar woman, and so I am here, too. And many here have given just one onion each, only one little onion.... What are all our deeds? And you, my gentle one, you, my kind boy, you also knew how to give an onion to a starving woman today. Begin your work, dear one, begin it, gentle one!... Do you see our Sun? Do you see Him?”

old: Oddly enough, you would have thought despair was all he had left. What chance did he have of raising such a sum, with nothing in the world? Yet right to the end he kept hoping he would get that three thousand, and that the money would somehow arrive of its own accord, as if it might fall from heaven. That is exactly how it is with people like Dmitri. The only dealings they have ever had with money was squandering what came to them by inheritance, with no effort on their part, and they have no idea how money is come by. As soon as he parted from Alyosha two days earlier, a whirl of the most fantastic notions seized his brain and tangled his thoughts in confusion. That is why he fixed first on a perfectly wild undertaking. And perhaps for men of that kind in such circumstances, the most impossible and fantastic schemes are the first to occur to them, and look the most practical.

old: Whatever one thinks of it, there was a great deal of simplicity in all this on Mitya’s part, for with all his vices he was a thoroughly simple-hearted man. Here is an example. Mitya seriously believed that old Kuzma, standing on the brink of the next world, must sincerely regret his past dealings with Grushenka. He believed that she had no more devoted friend and protector anywhere than this now harmless old man.

old: The upper floor had a number of large rooms that were kept purely for show and furnished in the old-fashioned merchant style. Dull, long rows of clumsy mahogany chairs stood against the walls, glass chandeliers hung under covers, and gloomy mirrors looked down from between the windows. None of these rooms were ever used. The old man lived in one small, remote bedroom, where an old servant woman with a kerchief on her head looked after him, along with a lad who sat on the chest out in the passage. His legs were so swollen that he could barely walk. Only now and then was he lifted out of his leather armchair, and then the old woman held him up and walked him once or twice up and down the room. He was sullen and silent even with her.

old: Mitya sat on a little chair near the entrance, waiting for his fate in nervous impatience. When the old man came in at the far door, seventy feet away, Mitya sprang up and went to meet him with his long, military stride. He was well dressed, in a buttoned-up frock-coat, with a round hat and black gloves in his hands. It was just how he had looked three days before at the elder’s, at the family meeting with his father and brothers. The old man stood waiting for him, dignified and unbending, and Mitya felt that the old man was sizing him up through and through as he came. He was also struck by Samsonov’s monstrously swollen face. The lower lip, always thick, now hung down like a bun. The old man bowed to his guest in dignified silence and waved him to a low chair by the sofa. Then, leaning on his son’s arm, he started to lower himself onto the sofa opposite, groaning with pain. Watching his struggle, Mitya at once felt remorse. He felt, too, how small he was in the presence of this dignified man he had dared to disturb.

old: “I never expected that much!” cried Mitya, ecstatic. (He was still in a state of ecstasy.) He seized his six roubles and ran home. There he borrowed three roubles from the people of the house. They were so fond of him that they handed it over gladly, though it was all they had. In his excitement Mitya told them right then that his fate would be decided that day. In desperate haste he described the whole scheme he had put to Samsonov, how Samsonov had decided, what he himself hoped for the future, and so on. These people had been told many of their lodger’s secrets before, so they saw him as a gentleman with no pride at all, almost one of themselves. Now that he had nine roubles, Mitya sent for posting-horses to take him to the Volovya station. This is how it came to be remembered and put on record that “at midday, on the day before the event, Mitya had not a farthing, and that he had sold his watch to get money and had borrowed three roubles from his landlord, all in the presence of witnesses.”

old: First, he was late. He took a short cut from Volovya station, and it turned out to be eighteen versts instead of twelve. Second, the priest was not at home in Ilyinskoe. He had gone off to a neighboring village. Mitya set out there with the same worn-out horses, and by the time he found the priest it was almost dark.

old: “He’ll be all right now.”
new: “It’ll be all right now.”

old: “No, you show me this: name me the law that allows roguery. D’you hear? You’re a scoundrel! Get that into your head!”
new: “No, you show me this: name me the law that allows roguery. D’you hear? You’re a scoundrel! Do you understand that?”

old: “You can tell me all that afterwards, afterwards!” Madame Hohlakov raised her hand and demanded silence in her turn. “And whatever you tell me, I know it all beforehand. I’ve said so already. You ask for a certain sum, three thousand, but I can give you more, immeasurably more. I will save you, Dmitri Fyodorovitch, but you must listen to me.”

old: “You’re lying!” shouted Mitya. “The way you’re shaking, I can tell you know where she is.”
new: “You’re lying!” shouted Mitya. “From your terror I know where she is.”

old: He rushed off. Fenya, in her fright, was glad to have got away so lightly. But she knew very well that he had only been in too much of a hurry, or she might not have fared so well. And as he ran, he startled both Fenya and old Matryona with something unexpected. On the table stood a brass mortar with a pestle in it, a small brass pestle, hardly more than six inches long. Mitya already had the door open with one hand when, with the other, he grabbed the pestle and shoved it into his coat pocket.

old: He settled on a different plan. He went a long way around Fyodor Pavlovitch’s house, crossed the lane, ran down Dmitrovsky Street and over the little bridge, and came out at the deserted alley behind the house. Nobody lived there and nobody ever passed. On one side was the wattle fence of a neighbor’s kitchen-garden. On the other was the tall, strong fence that ran all around Fyodor Pavlovitch’s garden. Here he chose a spot, apparently the very one where, as the story went and he knew it, Lizaveta had once climbed over. “If she could climb over it,” the thought came to him, God knows why, “surely I can.” He jumped up and at once got a grip on the top of the fence. Then he hauled himself up with all his strength and sat astride it. The bath-house stood close by in the garden, but from the fence he could also see the lit windows of the house.

old: “Tell me, now! Where is she? Who’s she with at Mokroe?” he roared furiously.
new: “Tell me, now! Where is she? Who’s she with now, at Mokroe?” he roared furiously.

old: “Oh, hell!” he said. “Haven’t you got some kind of rag ... to wipe my face?”
new: “Oh, damn it!” he said. “Haven’t you got some kind of rag ... to wipe my face?”

old: “To Plotnikov’s shop, splendid!” cried Mitya, as though an idea had struck him. “Misha,” he said to the boy as he came in, “listen, run over to Plotnikov’s and tell them Dmitri Fyodorovitch sends his greetings and will be there in a moment.... But listen, listen, tell them to have champagne ready before I come, three dozen bottles, packed the way it was when it went to Mokroe. I took four dozen with me that time,” he added (suddenly addressing Pyotr Ilyitch). “They know all about it, don’t you worry, Misha,” he said, turning to the boy again. “Wait, listen. Tell them to put in cheese, Strasburg pies, smoked fish, ham, caviare, and everything, everything they have, up to a hundred roubles, or a hundred and twenty like last time.... But wait, don’t let them forget dessert: sweets, pears, watermelons, two or three or four—no, one melon will do—and chocolate, candy, toffee, fondants. In fact, everything I took to Mokroe before, three hundred roubles’ worth with the champagne ... let it be exactly the same again. And remember, Misha, if your name really is Misha.... His name is Misha, isn’t it?” He turned to Pyotr Ilyitch again.

old: “Not coming? Well, I’ll knock them up, I will!” he muttered at each knock, fuming at himself. But at the same time he knocked even harder on the gate.

old: “Straight to hell?” Mitya broke in, and let out his short, abrupt laugh. “Andrey, simple soul,” and he grabbed him by the shoulders again, “tell me, what do you think, will Dmitri Fyodorovitch Karamazov go to hell or not?”

old: “Oh, sir! You frighten me, driving you, the way you talk is so odd.”
new: “Oh, sir! I’m afraid of driving you, the way you talk is so strange.”

old: “Some strangers. One is an official, a gentleman, a Pole by the sound of him. He’s the one who sent horses here to fetch her. And there’s another with him, a friend of his or a traveling companion, who can tell. They’re in civilian clothes.”

old: “Flying it went, sir. How could I forget? You must have left three thousand behind.”
new: “Flying it went. How could I forget? You must have left three thousand behind.”

old: Trifon Borissovitch gave Mitya a wary look, but at once did as he was told, without a word. He took him into the passage and went by himself into the first big room, next to the one where the guests sat, and carried away the light. Then he led Mitya in on tiptoe and set him in a dark corner, where he could watch the company freely without being seen. But Mitya did not look for long. In fact he could not see them at all. He saw her. His heart pounded, and everything went dark before his eyes.

old: “Gentlemen,” he said, loudly, almost shouting, yet stumbling over every word, “I ... I’m all right! Don’t be afraid!” he exclaimed. “I—nothing’s the matter,” he said, suddenly turning to Grushenka, who had shrunk back in her chair toward Kalganov and was gripping his hand. “I ... I’m staying, too. I’m here till morning. Gentlemen, may I stay with you till morning? Only till morning, one last time, in this very room?”

I’d like some myself, and I can’t bear liqueurs. And best of all, you’re here yourself. We were dreadfully bored.... Have you come on a spree again, I suppose? But put that money away. Where did you get so much?”

old: The Pole on the sofa impressed him with his dignified manner and his Polish accent, and most of all with his pipe. “Well, so what? It’s a good thing he smokes a pipe,” he thought. The Pole’s puffy, middle-aged face, with its tiny nose and its two very thin, pointed, dyed, cheeky-looking mustaches, hadn’t raised the slightest suspicion in Mitya so far. He wasn’t even particularly struck by the man’s ridiculous wig, made in Siberia, with love-locks combed foolishly forward over the temples. “It must be all right, since he wears a wig,” he went on, musing blissfully. The other Pole, the younger one, was staring at the company with insolent defiance and listening to the talk in silent contempt. He impressed Mitya only by his great height, which made a striking contrast with the Pole on the sofa. “If he stood up, he’d be six foot three.” The thought flitted through Mitya’s head. It also occurred to him that this man must be the other’s friend, a kind of “bodyguard,” and that the big Pole was no doubt at the little Pole with the pipe’s service. But all this seemed to Mitya perfectly proper and not to be questioned. In his doglike mood of submission, every feeling of rivalry had died out.

old: “What? He offered you money over me?” cried Grushenka, hysterical. “Is that true, Mitya? How dare you? Am I for sale?”
new: “What? He offered you money for me?” cried Grushenka, hysterical. “Is that true, Mitya? How dare you? Am I for sale?”

old: “Oh, him is it you’re after?” Grushenka laughed. “Stay here with me a minute. Mitya, go and find his Maximov for him.”
new: “So it’s him you’re after.” Grushenka laughed. “Stay here with me a minute. Mitya, go and find his Maximov for him.”

old: “In flew a falcon, and my heart dropped. ‘Fool, that’s the man you love!’ my heart whispered to me at once. Then you walked in and everything lit up. What’s he scared of? I wondered. You were frightened, you couldn’t say a word. You’re not afraid of those people—could you be scared of anyone? He’s afraid of me, I thought, only of me. So Fenya told you, you silly boy, that I called out of the window to Alyosha that I’d loved Mityenka for one hour, and that now I was off to love ... somebody else. Mitya, Mitya, what a fool I was, to think I could love anybody after you! Will you forgive me, Mitya? Do you forgive me or don’t you? Do you love me? Do you love me?” She leaped up and took him by the shoulders with both hands. Mitya, struck dumb with rapture, looked into her eyes, her face, her smile, and then suddenly crushed her in his arms and kissed her passionately.

old: “Me, drunk! I’m drunk anyway ... drunk on you ... and now I’ll get drunk on wine too.”

old: “You’re the _lajdak_! You’re a little scoundrel, that’s what.”
new: “You’re a _lajdak_ yourself! You’re a little scoundrel, that’s what you are.”

old: “N—no. But if you would write three lines in your own hand, saying that you did not give Dmitri Fyodorovitch any money, it might be of some use ... in case it’s needed....”

old: Mihail Makarovitch was not at all brilliant at his work, though he did it no worse than many others. To put it plainly, he had little education. He could not always be trusted to know where his official powers ended. He didn’t exactly fail to understand certain reforms of the present reign. Rather, he made glaring blunders when he applied them. This wasn’t because he was especially dull. He was careless, and always too hurried to look into the matter properly.

old: “I have the heart of a soldier, not a civilian,” he used to say of himself. He had never formed a clear idea of the basic principles behind the reforms that followed the emancipation of the serfs. He simply picked them up from year to year, so to speak, and added to what he knew through practice, without ever meaning to. And he was a landowner himself, too. Pyotr Ilyitch knew for certain that he would find some of Mihail Makarovitch’s visitors there that evening, but he didn’t know which ones. As it happened, the prosecutor was at that moment playing whist at the captain’s with Varvinsky, our district doctor. Varvinsky was a young man who had just come to us from Petersburg, where he had taken a brilliant degree at the Academy of Medicine. Ippolit Kirillovitch, the prosecutor, was really only the deputy prosecutor, but we always called him the prosecutor. He was a rather peculiar man, about thirty-five, inclined to consumption, and married to a fat, childless wife. He was vain and irritable, though he had a good mind and even a kind heart. The trouble with him seemed to be only this: he thought himself abler than he was. That kept him constantly ill at ease. He also had higher, even artistic, leanings, toward psychology for instance, toward a special study of the human heart and a special knowledge of the criminal and his crime. He felt wronged on this account. He believed he had been passed over in the service, and he was firmly convinced that in higher circles he was not properly valued and had enemies. In gloomy moments he even threatened to resign and take up criminal cases as a barrister. The unexpected Karamazov case stirred him deeply: “It was a case that might well be talked about all over Russia.” But I am running ahead.

old: But Marfa kept on screaming. She saw that her master’s window was open and a candle was alight in it, so she ran over and began calling Fyodor Pavlovitch. But when she looked in at the window, she saw a fearful sight. Her master lay on his back on the floor, not moving. His light-colored dressing gown and white shirt were soaked in blood. The candle on the table lit up the blood and the still, dead face of Fyodor Pavlovitch, brightly. Terror-stricken, Marfa rushed from the window and out of the garden. She drew the bolt of the big gate and ran headlong, by the back way, to the neighbor, Marya Kondratyevna. Mother and daughter were both asleep, but Marfa’s desperate, unceasing screams and her knocking at the shutter woke them. Shrieking and screaming incoherently, Marfa still managed to tell them the main fact and beg for help. As it happened, Foma had come back from his wanderings and was spending the night with them. They got him up at once, and all three ran to the scene of the crime. On the way Marya Kondratyevna remembered that about eight o’clock she had heard a dreadful scream from the garden next door. That must have been Grigory’s scream of “Parricide!”, uttered when he caught hold of Mitya’s leg.

old: I will say briefly that Fyodor Pavlovitch was found quite dead, his skull smashed in. But with what? Most probably with the same weapon that had struck Grigory. And the moment that weapon was found, Grigory, who was at once given all possible medical help, told in a weak, breaking voice how he had been knocked down. They searched with a lantern by the fence and found the brass pestle, dropped in a most conspicuous place on the garden path. In the room where Fyodor Pavlovitch lay, nothing showed any sign of a struggle. But by the bed, behind the screen, they picked up from the floor a big, thick envelope. On it was written: “A present of three thousand roubles for my angel Grushenka, if she is willing to come.” Below that Fyodor Pavlovitch had added, “For my little chicken.” The envelope bore three seals of red sealing wax, but it had been torn open and was empty: the money had been taken. On the floor they also found a piece of narrow pink ribbon, which had been tied around the envelope.

old: But the inquiry, the search and the formalities in Fyodor Pavlovitch’s house held them all up. It took time, and so they sent someone ahead to Mokroe two hours before they set out. This was the officer of the rural police, Mavriky Mavrikyevitch Schmertsov, who had come into town the morning before to collect his pay. His orders were not to raise the alarm when he reached Mokroe. He was to keep constant watch over the “criminal” until the proper authorities arrived, and to find witnesses for the arrest, police constables, and so on. Mavriky Mavrikyevitch did as he was told. He kept his identity secret and gave no one the slightest hint of his secret business, except his old acquaintance Trifon Borissovitch. He had spoken to him just before Mitya met the landlord on the balcony, looking for him in the dark, and he noticed at once a change in Trifon Borissovitch’s face and voice. So neither Mitya nor anyone else knew he was being watched. Trifon Borissovitch had carried off the box with the pistols and put it in a safe place. Only after four o’clock, almost at sunrise, did all the officials arrive, the police captain, the prosecutor and the investigating lawyer, in two carriages each drawn by three horses. The doctor stayed behind at Fyodor Pavlovitch’s, to carry out a post-mortem on the body next day. But he was especially interested in the condition of the servant, Smerdyakov.

old: “I’m innocent! I didn’t shed that blood! I’m not guilty of my father’s blood.... I meant to kill him, yes. But I’m innocent. It wasn’t me.”
new: “I’m not guilty! I’m not guilty of that blood! I’m not guilty of my father’s blood.... I meant to kill him, yes. But I’m not guilty. Not I.”

old: “Yes, it’s your fault! You’re the chief criminal! You fury! You harlot! You’re the one most to blame!” shouted the police captain, shaking his fist at her. But he was stopped at once, and firmly. The prosecutor simply grabbed him.
new: “Yes, it’s your fault! You’re the chief criminal! You fury! You harlot! You’re the one most to blame!” shouted the police captain, threatening her with his hand. But he was stopped at once, and firmly. The prosecutor simply grabbed him.

old: “I will gladly take your sensible advice,” the prosecutor interposed, addressing Mitya. “But I am not withdrawing my question. It is vitally important for us now to know exactly why you needed that sum, I mean precisely three thousand.”
new: “I will follow your sensible advice entirely,” the prosecutor interposed, addressing Mitya. “But I am not withdrawing my question. It is vitally important for us now to know exactly why you needed that sum, I mean precisely three thousand.”

old: “The devil take the pestle!” burst from him suddenly.
new: “Blast the pestle!” burst from him suddenly.

old: “They’re angry and offended,” he thought. “Well, to hell with them!”
new: “They’re angry and offended,” he thought. “Well, forget them!”

old: “Next? Why, next I killed him ... hit him on the head and cracked his skull.... That’s your version, I suppose. That’s it!”
new: “Next? Why, next I murdered him ... hit him on the head and cracked his skull.... That’s your version, I suppose. That’s it!”

old: “Oh, damn it!... I jumped down to get a look at the man I’d hurt ... I couldn’t tell you why!”
new: “Oh, blast it!... I jumped down to get a look at the man I’d hurt ... I couldn’t tell you why!”

old: “Look, gentlemen, joking aside”—Mitya raised his eyes and looked at them both steadily—“I had a feeling from the very beginning that we’d come to blows at this point. But at first, when I started giving my evidence, it was all still far off and hazy; it was all floating about, and I was so naive that I began by assuming we trusted each other. Now I can see for myself that there can be no such trust, because sooner or later we were bound to run into this cursed stumbling-block. And now we’ve run into it! It’s impossible, and that’s the end of it! But I don’t blame you. You can’t believe it all just because I say so. I understand that, of course.”

old: “What, I’m to sit here naked?” he shouted.
new: “What, am I to stay naked?” he shouted.

old: “So am I to sit here naked like this?” he added savagely.
new: “So am I to stay naked like this?” he added savagely.

old: “To hell with his sorrow! Well, where to now? Do I just go on sitting here?”
new: “Damn his sorrow! Well, where to now? Do I just go on sitting here?”

old: “But you told us yourself that the envelope was under your father’s pillow, God rest him. You specifically said it was under the pillow, so you must have known.”
new: “But you told us yourself that the envelope was under your late father’s pillow. You specifically said it was under the pillow, so you must have known.”

old: Mitya was beyond description agitated. He went pale.
new: Mitya was indescribably agitated. He went pale.

old: “Why were you so reticent? Why did you make such a secret of it? To put it more exactly: you have now told us your secret, which you yourself call ‘disgraceful.’ Yet in reality—comparatively speaking, of course—this act, the taking of three thousand roubles belonging to someone else, and only for a time, naturally, is in my view merely extreme recklessness, and not so disgraceful, given your character.... Grant that it was highly discreditable. Still, discreditable is not ‘disgraceful.’... Many people have guessed during this last month that you spent Katerina Ivanovna’s three thousand, and I heard the tale myself, quite apart from your confession.... Mihail Makarovitch, for one, had heard it as well, so that it was hardly a tale any more, just the gossip of the whole town. There are also signs, if I am not mistaken, that you admitted this yourself to somebody, I mean that the money was Katerina Ivanovna’s. So I am greatly surprised that up to this moment you have made such an extraordinary secret of the fifteen hundred you say you set aside, and have attached a feeling of positive horror to that secret.... It is hard to believe that confessing it could cost you such anguish.... Just now you cried out that Siberia would be better than confessing it ...”

old: “Yes, I see a vital difference! Any man can be a scoundrel, and probably every man is one, but not everyone can be a thief. For that you have to be an arch-scoundrel. Oh, of course, I don’t know how to draw these fine lines ... but a thief is lower than a scoundrel, that’s what I believe. Listen: I carry the money on me for a whole month. Any day I might make up my mind to give it back, and then I’m not a scoundrel anymore. But I can’t make up my mind, you see, though I decide every day, every day I push myself to do it, and still for a whole month I can’t bring myself to it. Is that right, do you think? Is that right?”

old: “Oh, how low that would have been! Gentlemen, do you know, you’re torturing me! All right, I’ll tell you everything. I’ll confess all my infernal wickedness, but only to put you to shame. You’ll be amazed yourselves at the depths of disgrace a jumble of human passions can sink to. You should know that I had that plan myself, the one you just mentioned, prosecutor! Yes, gentlemen, that thought has been in my head all this month too. I was on the point of deciding to go to Katya—I was mean enough for that. But think of it! To go to her, to tell her about my treachery, and then to beg money from her, from Katya (to beg, do you hear, to beg), to pay for that very treachery. And then to go straight from her to run away with the other woman, her rival, who hated her and insulted her! You must be mad, prosecutor!”

I’d have taken it, oh yes, I’d have taken the money, and then for the rest of my life ... oh, God! Forgive me, gentlemen, I’m shouting like this because the thought has been in my mind so recently, only the day before yesterday, that night when I was having all that trouble with Lyagavy, and then all day yesterday, I remember, right up until that happened ...”

And will they forgive me in the next world or not?’”
new: They questioned all the peasants Trifon Borissovitch had named: Stepan and Semyon, the driver Andrey, and Kalganov. The peasants and the driver backed up Trifon Borissovitch’s story without a moment’s doubt. They wrote down with special care Andrey’s report of what Mitya had said to him on the road: “‘Where am I going,’ he says, ‘Dmitri Fyodorovitch, to heaven or to hell? And shall I be forgiven in the next world or not?’”

old: “Gentlemen, we’re all cruel, we’re all monsters, we all make men weep, and mothers, and babes at the breast. But let it be settled here, now: of all of us, I am the lowest reptile! I swore to reform, and every day I’ve gone on doing the same filthy things. I understand now that men like me need a blow, a blow of destiny to catch them like a noose and bind them by a force from outside. Never, never would I have risen by myself! But the thunderbolt has fallen. I accept the torture of the accusation and my public shame. I want to suffer, and by suffering I will be purified. Perhaps I will be purified, gentlemen? But listen, for the last time: I am not guilty of my father’s blood. I accept my punishment, not because I killed him, but because I meant to kill him, and I might really have killed him. Still, I mean to fight it out with you. I warn you of that. I’ll fight it out with you to the end, and then God will decide. Good-by, gentlemen. Don’t be angry with me for shouting at you during the examination. Oh, I was such a fool then.... In another minute I’ll be a prisoner, but now, for the last time, as a free man, Dmitri Karamazov offers you his hand. In saying good-by to you, I say it to all men.”

old: “I’ll thank you to learn how to speak to me, if nobody’s ever taught you. I’m not ‘old fellow’ to you, and you can keep your advice for another time!” Mavriky Mavrikyevitch snapped savagely, as though glad to vent his anger.

old: “Oh, no. Some people have deep feelings and have somehow been crushed. In them, buffoonery is a bitter irony aimed at the people they’re afraid to tell the truth, because for years those people have humiliated and cowed them. Believe me, Krassotkin, that kind of buffoonery can be tragic in the extreme. His whole life now is centered on Ilusha. If Ilusha dies, he will either go mad with grief or kill himself. I’m almost sure of it when I look at him now.”

He shouted hurriedly to Smurov, “Open the door!” and the moment it was open he blew his whistle. Perezvon came tearing into the room.

old: Startling news has reached our class: Kolbasnikov has turned out an ass.
new: Astounding news has reached the class, Kolbasnikov has been an ass.

old: “He knows everything, father, he knows more than any of us!” put in Ilusha. “He only acts like he doesn’t, but really he’s top in every subject....”
new: “He knows everything, father, he knows more than any of us!” put in Ilusha. “He only acts like that, but really he’s top in every subject....”

old: “And you torment everyone around you,” smiled Alyosha.
new: “And you worry everyone around you,” smiled Alyosha.

old: “Yes, I torment everyone around me, especially my mother. Karamazov, tell me, am I very ridiculous now?”
new: “Yes, I worry everyone around me, especially my mother. Karamazov, tell me, am I very ridiculous now?”

old: “Sicily! Your Excellency,” the captain stammered, “but you’ve seen how we live”—he spread out his hands at the room around him—“with mamma and the whole family?”

old: “I don’t want a good boy! I don’t want another boy!” he muttered in a wild whisper, grinding his teeth. “If I forget thee, Jerusalem, may my tongue—” His voice broke in a sob, and he dropped to his knees before the wooden bench. He pressed his fists to his head and began to sob with strange, whimpering cries, struggling to keep them from being heard in the room.

old: Alyosha was heading across the cathedral square to the widow Morozov’s house, to see Grushenka. She had sent Fenya to him early that morning with an urgent message asking him to come. Fenya told him, when he questioned her, that her mistress had been particularly upset since the day before. In the two months since Mitya’s arrest, Alyosha had often visited the widow Morozov’s house, partly because he wished to and partly to carry messages for Mitya. Three days after Mitya was arrested, Grushenka had fallen gravely ill, and she remained ill for almost five weeks. For one whole week she had lain unconscious. She had changed a great deal. She was thinner and a little sallow, although for the last fortnight she had been well enough to go out. Yet to Alyosha her face was more attractive than ever, and he liked meeting her eyes when he came in. Her face had taken on a look of firmness and intelligent purpose. Something in her had been transformed inside, and one could see in her a quiet, fine, humble determination that nothing could shake. A small vertical line had appeared between her brows, and at first glance it gave her charming face a thoughtful, almost stern look. Hardly a trace remained of her old frivolity.

old: Alyosha had not been there for four days, and he was in a hurry to go straight up to Lise, because she was the one he needed to talk to. Lise had sent a maid to him the day before with a special request that he come and see her “about something very important,” and for certain reasons that request interested Alyosha. But while the maid was gone to announce him to Lise, Madame Hohlakov heard from someone that he had arrived and at once sent a message begging him to come to her “for just one minute.” Alyosha decided it was best to give in to the mamma’s request, or else she would keep sending down to Lise’s room every minute he was there. Madame Hohlakov was lying on her couch. She was dressed with particular elegance and was obviously in a state of extreme nervous excitement. She greeted Alyosha with cries of delight.

old: “I can sit up. Oh, you’ve muddled me! Oh, this trial, this savage deed, and then they’re all off to Siberia, some are getting married, and all of it so fast, so fast, everything changing, and in the end—nothing. Everybody grows old with death ahead of them. Well, so be it! I’m weary. Katya, that _cette charmante personne_, has let down all my hopes. Now she’s going to follow one of your brothers to Siberia, and your other brother is going to follow her and settle in the nearest town, and they’ll all torment one another. It drives me out of my mind. Worst of all is the publicity. The story has been told a million times in all the papers in Moscow and Petersburg. Oh, and would you believe it, one of them says I was ‘a dear friend’ of your brother’s ——, I can’t bring myself to say the horrid word. Just fancy, just fancy!”

old: “Well, then, I’ll tell you everything. It can’t be helped, I’ll make a confession, since there is one point where I may have been at fault. Only a tiny, tiny point, so tiny it hardly counts. You see, my dear boy”—Madame Hohlakov suddenly turned arch, and a charming, enigmatic smile played on her lips—“you see, I suspect ... You must forgive me, Alyosha. I’m like a mother to you.... No, no, just the opposite. I’m speaking to you now as if you were my father—mother is quite out of place. Well, it’s as though I were confessing to Father Zossima, that’s exactly it. I called you a monk just now. So then, that poor young man, your friend Rakitin (Mercy on us! I can’t be angry with him. I’m cross, but not very), that frivolous young man, would you believe it, seems to have got it into his head that he’s in love with me. I only noticed later. At first, a month ago, he merely began coming to see me more often, nearly every day, though of course we knew each other before. I suspected nothing ... and then all at once it dawned on me, and I started noticing things, with astonishment. You know, two months ago that modest, charming, excellent young man, Pyotr Ilyitch Perhotin, who’s in the service here, became a regular visitor. You’ve met him here ever so many times yourself. And he’s such an excellent, serious young man, isn’t he? He comes once every three days, not daily (though I’d be glad to see him daily), and always so well dressed. In short, I love young people, Alyosha, talented and modest ones, like you. And he has nearly a statesman’s mind, he talks so charmingly, and I’ll certainly, certainly try to get him promoted. He’s a diplomat in the making. On that awful day he almost saved me from death by coming in the night. And your friend Rakitin turns up in such boots, and always stretches them out on the carpet.... Then he began to hint at his feelings, and one day as he was leaving he squeezed my hand terribly hard. My foot began to swell right after he’d pressed my hand like that. He’d met Pyotr Ilyitch here before, and would you believe it, he’s forever sneering at him, snarling at him, for no reason I can see. I simply watched the two of them together and laughed to myself. So I was sitting here alone—no, I was laid up then. Well, I was lying here alone when suddenly in comes Rakitin, and just fancy! He’d brought me some verses of his own writing—a little poem about my bad foot, that is, he’d described my foot in a poem. Wait a moment—how did it go?

old: “Aberration of what?” Alyosha asked, bewildered.
new: “What aberration?” Alyosha asked, bewildered.

old: “I’ll tell you. This Katya ... Ah! She’s a charming, charming creature, but I can never make out who she’s in love with. She was here a while back and I couldn’t get a word out of her. All the more because now she only chats with me about trifles. It’s my health, my health, nothing else, and what a tone she takes with me! So I just said to myself, ‘Well, so be it. I don’t care’... Oh, yes. I was talking about aberration. The doctor has arrived. You know a doctor has arrived? Of course you do—the one who finds out who is mad. You sent for him. No, not you, it was Katya. It’s all Katya’s doing. Now, you see, a man can sit there perfectly sane and all at once have an aberration. He may be fully aware and know what he’s doing, and still be in a state of aberration. And there’s no doubt that Dmitri Fyodorovitch was suffering from aberration. People found out about aberration the moment the law courts were reformed. That is all the good the reformed courts have done. The doctor was here and asked me about that evening, about the gold mines. ‘How did he seem then?’ he asked. He must have been in a state of aberration. He burst in shouting, ‘Money, money, three thousand! Give me three thousand!’ and then he left and did the murder straight away. ‘I don’t want to murder him,’ he said, and suddenly he went and murdered him. That is why they will acquit him: he fought against it, and yet he murdered him.”
