old: “From aberration. When he came round from the blow Dmitri Fyodorovitch gave him on the head, he was in a state of aberration, and he went and did the murder. As for his saying he didn’t, very likely he just doesn’t remember. Only, you know, it would be better, ever so much better, if it was Dmitri Fyodorovitch who murdered him. And that’s how it must have been, though I keep saying Grigory. It was certainly Dmitri Fyodorovitch, and that’s better, ever so much better! Oh! I don’t mean it’s better that a son should kill his father. I don’t defend that. Children should honor their parents. And yet it would be better if it were he, because then you’d have nothing to weep over, since he did it unconscious—or rather conscious, but without knowing what he was doing. Let them acquit him! That is so humane, and it would show what a blessing the reformed courts are. I knew nothing about all this, but they say the courts have been reformed for a long time. When I heard of it yesterday I was so struck that I wanted to send for you at once. And if he’s acquitted, make him come straight from the courtroom to dine with me. I’ll invite a party of friends and we’ll drink to the reformed courts. I don’t think he’d be dangerous. Besides, I’ll ask a great many friends, so that he could always be led out if he tried anything. And afterwards he could be made a justice of the peace somewhere in another town, since those who have been in trouble themselves make the best judges. And anyway, who isn’t suffering from aberration these days?—you, I, all of us are in a state of aberration, and there are plenty of examples. A man sits singing a song, something suddenly annoys him, he picks up a pistol and shoots the first person he sees, and nobody blames him. I read that recently, and all the doctors confirm it. The doctors are forever confirming; they’ll confirm anything. Why, my Lise is in a state of aberration. She made me cry again yesterday, and the day before, and today I suddenly saw that it’s all aberration. Oh, Lise grieves me so! I think she is completely mad. Why did she send for you? Did she send for you, or did you come of your own accord?”

old: “Oh, yes. You won’t forget what I asked you, will you? It’s a matter of life and death!”

old: “I was listening at the door. Why are you staring at me? I wanted to listen, so I did. What’s wrong with that? I won’t say sorry.”
new: “I was listening. Why are you staring at me? I wanted to listen, so I did. What’s wrong with that? I won’t say sorry.”

old: “I wanted to tell you something I long for. I’d like somebody to torment me. To marry me and then torment me, to cheat on me and leave. I don’t want to be happy.”
new: “I wanted to tell you something I long for. I’d like somebody to torture me. To marry me and then torture me, to deceive me and leave. I don’t want to be happy.”

old: “There’s a book here where I read about the trial of a Jew. He took a four-year-old child and cut the fingers off both its hands. Then he crucified the child on a wall, driving nails into it, and afterwards, at his trial, he said the child had died soon, within four hours. ‘Soon,’ he called that! He said the child moaned and went on moaning, and he stood there admiring it. That’s nice!”
new: “There’s a book here where I read about the trial of a Jew. He took a child of four years old and cut the fingers off both hands. Then he crucified him on a wall, hammered nails into him and crucified him, and afterwards, at his trial, he said the child had died soon, within four hours. ‘Soon,’ he called that! He said the child moaned and went on moaning, and he stood there admiring it. That’s nice!”

old: It was quite late when Alyosha rang at the prison gate. Days are short in November, and dusk was already coming on. But Alyosha knew he would be let in without trouble. Our little town handled such things the way every town does. At first, once the preliminary inquiry was over, relatives and a few other people could see Mitya only after going through certain unavoidable formalities. Later the formalities stayed in place, but exceptions were made for some of Mitya’s visitors, at least. So many, in fact, that the meetings with the prisoner in the room set aside for them were sometimes practically _tête-à-tête_.

old: These exceptions were few, though. Only Grushenka, Alyosha and Rakitin were treated this way. The police captain, Mihail Mihailovitch, was very favorably inclined toward Grushenka. The way he had abused her at Mokroe lay heavy on the old man’s conscience, and when he learned the whole story he changed his opinion of her entirely. And strange to say, he was firmly convinced of Mitya’s guilt, yet once Mitya was in prison the old man judged him more and more mildly. “Perhaps he was a good-hearted man,” he thought, “who came to grief through drink and dissipation.” His first horror had turned into pity. As for Alyosha, the captain was very fond of him and had known him for a long time. Rakitin had recently begun visiting the prisoner very often. He was one of the closest acquaintances of “the police captain’s young ladies,” as the captain called them, and was always hanging about their house. He also gave lessons at the house of the prison superintendent. The superintendent was strict in carrying out his duties, but he was a kind old man. Alyosha had known him well for years, and the old man liked talking with him, usually about sacred subjects. He respected Ivan Fyodorovitch and stood in awe of his opinion, though he was a bit of a philosopher himself, “self-taught,” of course. But Alyosha drew him irresistibly. This past year the old man had started studying the Apocryphal Gospels, and he was forever discussing his impressions with his young friend. He used to visit Alyosha at the monastery and talk for hours with him and with the monks. So even when Alyosha came late to the prison, he only had to go to the superintendent and everything was made easy. Besides, everyone in the prison, down to the lowliest warder, had grown used to Alyosha. And the sentry, naturally, gave him no trouble so long as the authorities were satisfied.
new: These exceptions were few, though. Only Grushenka, Alyosha and Rakitin were treated this way. The police captain, Mihail Mihailovitch, was very favorably inclined toward Grushenka. The way he had abused her at Mokroe lay heavy on the old man’s conscience, and when he learned the whole story he changed his opinion of her entirely. And strange to say, he was firmly convinced of Mitya’s guilt, yet once Mitya was in prison the old man judged him more and more mildly. “Perhaps he was a good-hearted man,” he thought, “who came to grief through drink and dissipation.” His first horror had turned into pity. As for Alyosha, the captain was very fond of him and had known him for a long time. Rakitin had recently begun visiting the prisoner very often. He was one of the closest acquaintances of “the police captain’s young ladies,” as the captain called them, and was always hanging about their house. He also gave lessons at the house of the prison superintendent. The superintendent was strict in carrying out his duties, but he was a kind old man. Alyosha had known him well for years, and the old man liked talking with him, usually about sacred subjects. He respected Ivan Fyodorovitch and stood in awe of his opinion, though he was a great philosopher himself, “self-taught,” of course. But Alyosha drew him irresistibly. This past year the old man had started studying the Apocryphal Gospels, and he was forever discussing his impressions with his young friend. He used to visit Alyosha at the monastery and talk for hours with him and with the monks. So even when Alyosha came late to the prison, he only had to go to the superintendent and everything was made easy. Besides, everyone in the prison, down to the lowliest warder, had grown used to Alyosha. And the sentry, naturally, gave him no trouble so long as the authorities were satisfied.

old: A captivating little foot, Though swollen and red and tender! The doctors come with plasters to put, But still they cannot mend her.
new: A captivating little foot, Though swollen and red and tender! The doctors come and plasters put, But still they cannot mend her.

old: Yet it’s not her foot that fills me with dread— That’s a theme for Pushkin’s muse, I suppose— It’s not her foot, it is her head: I tremble for the wits she loses!
new: Yet it’s not for her foot I dread— A theme for Pushkin’s muse more fit— It’s not her foot, it is her head: I tremble for her loss of wit!

old: For as her foot swells, strange to say, Her intellect begins to wane— Oh, for some cure, I beg and plead, To heal both foot and brain indeed!
new: For as her foot swells, strange to say, Her intellect is on the wane— Oh, for some remedy I pray That may restore both foot and brain!

old: “Rakitin wouldn’t understand this,” he began in a kind of exaltation. “But you, you’ll understand it all. That’s why I was thirsting for you. You see, there’s so much I’ve wanted to tell you for ever so long, here, inside these peeling walls. But I haven’t said a word about what matters most. The moment never seemed to come. Now I can’t wait any longer. I have to pour my heart out to you. Brother, in these last two months I’ve found a new man in myself. A new man has risen up in me. He was hidden inside me, and he would never have come to the surface if it hadn’t been for this blow from heaven. I’m afraid! And what do I care if I spend twenty years in the mines, breaking ore with a hammer? I’m not afraid of that at all. It’s something else I’m afraid of now: that the new man may leave me. Even there, in the mines, underground, I may find a human heart in another convict and murderer next to me, and I may make friends with him. Even there a man can live and love and suffer. You can thaw out a frozen heart in that convict, you can wait on him for years, and at last bring up from the dark depths a lofty soul, a feeling, suffering creature. You can bring forth an angel, create a hero! There are so many of them, hundreds of them, and we’re all to blame for them. Why did I dream of that ‘babe’ at such a moment? ‘Why is the babe so poor?’ That was a sign to me at that moment. It’s for the babe that I’m going. Because we’re all responsible for all. For all the ‘babes,’ because there are big children as well as little children. All are ‘babes.’ I go for all, because someone has to go for all. I didn’t kill father, but I have to go. I accept it. It all came to me here, here, inside these peeling walls. There are masses of them down there, hundreds of them underground, with hammers in their hands. Oh, yes, we’ll be in chains and there’ll be no freedom, but then, in our great sorrow, we’ll rise again to joy, without which man cannot live nor God exist, for God gives joy: it’s His privilege—a grand one. Ah, man should be dissolved in prayer! What would I be down there underground without God? Rakitin’s laughing! If they drive God from the earth, we’ll shelter Him underground. A man can’t exist in prison without God; it’s even more impossible than outside prison. And then we men underground will sing out of the bowels of the earth a glorious hymn to God, with Whom is joy. Hail to God and His joy! I love Him!”

old: “Yes, life is full. There’s life even underground,” he started again. “You won’t believe it, Alexey, but how I want to live now! Inside these peeling walls a hunger for existence and awareness has come over me. Rakitin can’t grasp that. All he wants is to build a house and rent out apartments. But you, I’ve been longing for you. And what is suffering anyway? I’m not afraid of it, even if there were no end to it. I’m not afraid of it now. I was before. Do you know, maybe I won’t answer a single question at the trial.... And I feel such strength in me now that I could bear anything, any pain at all, as long as I can say it to myself every moment: ‘I exist.’ In a thousand agonies—I exist. Stretched on the rack—I exist! Alone on top of a pillar—I exist! I see the sun, and if I can’t see the sun, I know it’s there. And a whole life lies in that, in knowing the sun is there. Alyosha, my angel, all these philosophies are the death of me. Damn them! Brother Ivan—”

old: “Who? You mean that fairy tale about the half-witted epileptic, Smerdyakov?”
new: “Who? You mean that fairy tale about the crazy idiot, the epileptic, Smerdyakov?”

old: “No, Ivan. You have told yourself many times that you are the murderer.”
new: “No, Ivan. You have told yourself several times that you are the murderer.”

old: But Ivan did not answer. Alyosha stood under the lamp-post at the crossroads until Ivan had disappeared into the dark. Then he turned and walked slowly home. Both Alyosha and Ivan lived in lodgings, since neither would live in Fyodor Pavlovitch’s empty house. Alyosha rented a furnished room from some working people. Ivan lived some distance off. He had taken a roomy, fairly comfortable lodge in the grounds of a fine house, owned by a well-to-do lady, an official’s widow. His only servant was a deaf, rheumatic old crone who went to bed at six every evening and rose at six every morning. Ivan had lately become remarkably careless of comfort, and very fond of solitude. He did everything for himself in the single room he lived in, and he seldom set foot in any other room of the lodge.

old: “The cellar was somewhere I had to go anyway, sir, several times a day,” Smerdyakov drawled slowly. “A year ago I fell out of the garret in just the same way. It’s true enough that nobody can tell the day and the hour of a fit beforehand, but you can always have a foreboding.”

old: “That was simply out of affection and sincere devotion to you, sir. I saw trouble coming in the house and wanted to spare you. But I wanted to spare myself even more. That’s why I told you to keep out of harm’s way, so you’d understand there’d be trouble in the house and stay at home to protect your father.”

old: “How could I say it straight out then, sir? It was only my fear that made me speak at all, and you might have been angry too. I could well have been afraid that Dmitri Fyodorovitch would make a scene and take that money, since he thought of it as practically his own. But who could have told it would end in a murder like this? I thought he’d only take the three thousand under the master’s mattress, in the envelope, and look, he has murdered him. How could you have guessed it either, sir?”

How could you have guessed it either, sir?”

old: “But at the time I thought you’d fully guessed, sir,” Smerdyakov countered with a perfectly innocent air.
new: “But at the time I thought you’d fully guessed,” Smerdyakov countered with a perfectly innocent air.

old: “Forgive me, sir, I thought you were the same as me.”
new: “Forgive me, I thought you were the same as me.”

old: “Out of plain simplicity, sir. I’ve never faked a fit on purpose in my life. I only said it to boast to you. It was just foolish. I liked you so much then, and I was frank with you.”
new: “Out of plain simplicity. I’ve never faked a fit on purpose in my life. I only said it to boast to you. It was just foolish. I liked you so much then, and I was frank with you.”

old: “I’m very grateful for everything, sir. Marfa Ignatyevna doesn’t forget me, and out of her kindness she gets me anything I need. Good people visit me every day.”
new: “I’m very grateful for everything. Marfa Ignatyevna doesn’t forget me, and out of her kindness she gets me anything I need. Good people visit me every day.”

old: “I quite understand, sir. And if you say nothing about that, I’ll say nothing about our conversation at the gate.”
new: “I quite understand. And if you say nothing about that, I’ll say nothing about our conversation at the gate.”

old: His main feeling was relief that the murderer was Mitya and not Smerdyakov, though you would have expected the reverse. He did not want to analyze why, and in fact felt a real reluctance to pry into his own feelings. He seemed to want to hurry up and forget something. Over the next few days he became convinced of Mitya’s guilt, as he learned how heavy the evidence against him was. Some of it came from unimportant people, Fenya and her mother for example, yet its effect was almost crushing. As for Perhotin, the people at the tavern and at Plotnikov’s shop, and the witnesses at Mokroe, their evidence looked conclusive. It was the details that did the damage. The secret of the knocks impressed the lawyers nearly as much as Grigory’s evidence about the open door. Grigory’s wife, Marfa, answering Ivan’s questions, declared that Smerdyakov had lain all night on the other side of the partition wall. “He was not three paces from our bed.” She was a sound sleeper, yet she had woken several times and heard him groaning. “He was groaning the whole time, groaning without a stop.”

old: But at that time something quite different was taking up most of his mind. On his return from Moscow he had given himself up, hopelessly, to a mad and consuming passion for Katerina Ivanovna. This is not the place to begin on that new passion of Ivan’s, which left its mark on the whole rest of his life. It would make the subject of another novel, which I may never write. But I cannot leave out one thing here. When Ivan, as I’ve already related, left Katerina Ivanovna with Alyosha and told him, “I am not keen on her,” it was an absolute lie. He loved her madly, though at times he hated her so much that he could have murdered her. Many causes helped to produce this feeling. Shattered by what had happened with Mitya, she had thrown herself on Ivan’s return into meeting him, as her one salvation. She had been hurt, insulted and humiliated in her feelings. And now back to her had come the man who had loved her so ardently before (oh! she knew that very well), and whose heart and intellect she thought far superior to her own. But the sternly virtuous girl did not surrender altogether to the man she loved, in spite of the Karamazov violence of his passions and the great fascination he had for her. At the same time she was constantly tormented by remorse for having deserted Mitya, and in moments of discord and violent anger (and there were plenty) she told Ivan so plainly. This was what he had meant when he told Alyosha, “lies upon lies.” There was, of course, much that was false in it, and that angered Ivan more than anything.... But of all this later.

old: “And it was true. There was no guessing about it. But didn’t you also suppose that what I wanted was just ‘one reptile devouring another’; that is, that Dmitri should kill father, and soon ... and that I myself was even ready to help it along?”

old: “Thanks,” snapped Ivan, and he left Alyosha and hurried on his way. From then on Alyosha noticed that Ivan clearly avoided him and even seemed to have taken a dislike to him, so much so that Alyosha stopped going to see him. After that meeting Ivan did not go home at all but went straight back to Smerdyakov.

old: “Nobody can hear anything. You’ve seen for yourself, sir: there’s a passage.”
new: “Nobody can hear anything. You’ve seen for yourself: there’s a passage.”

old: “I’ve got all my wits about me, sir, every one.”
new: “I’m in perfect possession of all my faculties.”

old: “By ‘something else’ I meant, sir, that you most likely wanted your parent dead as well. Very much so.”
new: “By ‘something else’ I meant that you, most likely, were very eager for your parent’s death as well.”

old: “I didn’t know what thoughts were in your mind then, sir,” said Smerdyakov resentfully. “And so I stopped you at the gate then to sound you out on that very point.”
new: “I didn’t know what thoughts were in your mind then,” said Smerdyakov resentfully. “And so I stopped you at the gate then to sound you out on that very point.”

old: “Why, that very matter, sir: whether you wanted your father murdered or not.”
new: “Why, that very matter: whether you wanted your father murdered or not.”

old: “You know for a fact, sir, that it wasn’t me who murdered him. And I’d have thought a sensible man had no need to bring it up again.”
new: “You know for a fact that it wasn’t me who murdered him. And I’d have thought a sensible man had no need to bring it up again.”

old: “As you already know, sir, it was simply from fear. I was in such a position, shaking with fear, that I suspected everyone. I decided to sound you out too, because I thought: if you wanted the same as your brother, then the business was as good as settled, and I would be crushed like a fly as well.”

old: “Is that all! Come on, answer me, I insist: what was it ... what could I possibly have done to plant such a degrading suspicion in your mean little soul?”
new: “What next! Come on, answer me, I insist: what was it ... what could I possibly have done to plant such a degrading suspicion in your mean soul?”

old: “What reason, sir? What about the inheritance?” said Smerdyakov sarcastically, and somehow vengefully. “After your parent’s death there was at least forty thousand to come to each of you, and very likely more. But if Fyodor Pavlovitch had married that lady, Agrafena Alexandrovna, she would have had all his capital transferred to her right after the wedding, for she has plenty of sense. Your parent wouldn’t have left the three of you two roubles. And were they far from a wedding, either? Not by a hair’s breadth. That lady had only to lift her little finger and he would have run after her to church with his tongue hanging out.”

old: “How could you help counting on him, sir? If he killed him, he would lose all the rights of a nobleman, his rank and his property, and go off into exile. So his share of the inheritance would come to you and your brother Alexey Fyodorovitch in equal parts. You would each get not forty but sixty thousand. There’s no doubt at all that you counted on Dmitri Fyodorovitch.”

So his share of the inheritance would come to you and your brother Alexey Fyodorovitch in equal parts. You would each get not forty but sixty thousand. There’s no doubt at all that you counted on Dmitri Fyodorovitch.”

old: “It was all that business of going to Tchermashnya, sir. Why, you were meaning to go to Moscow, and you refused all your father’s pleading to go to Tchermashnya—and then at one foolish word from me you agreed at once! What reason did you have to agree to Tchermashnya? You went to Tchermashnya for no reason, simply on my word. That shows you must have expected something from me.”

old: “You didn’t, sir? Then, as your father’s son, you should have had me hauled off to the lock-up and thrashed for what I said then ... or at the very least given me a punch in the face on the spot. But you weren’t the least bit angry, if you please. You at once acted, in the friendliest way, on my foolish word and went away. That was utterly absurd, for you ought to have stayed to save your parent’s life. How could I help drawing my conclusions?”

old: “In the ordinary occasions of life, sir,” he said, in the same smug, sententious tone in which he had taunted Grigory and argued with him about religion at Fyodor Pavlovitch’s table, “in the ordinary occasions of life, blows on the face are forbidden by law nowadays, and people have given them up. But in exceptional occasions of life people still fly to blows, not only among us but all over the world, even in the fullest Republic of France, just as in the time of Adam and Eve. And they never will leave off. But you, sir, even in an exceptional case, did not dare.”

new: “Why shouldn’t I learn them, to improve my education? I might happen to go some day to those happy parts of Europe myself.”

old: “To my mind, sir, you’d do better to keep quiet. What can you accuse me of, when I’m perfectly innocent? And who would believe you? Only, if you start, I’ll tell everything too, because I have to defend myself.”
new: “To my mind, you’d do better to keep quiet. What can you accuse me of, when I’m perfectly innocent? And who would believe you? Only, if you start, I’ll tell everything too, because I have to defend myself.”

old: “Even if the court doesn’t believe all I’ve just told you, sir, the public will, and then you will be the one ashamed.”
new: “Even if the court doesn’t believe all I’ve just told you, the public will, and then you will be the one ashamed.”

old: “Exactly right, sir. And you’d better be sensible.”
new: “Exactly right. And you’d better be sensible.”

old: FATAL KATYA: To-morrow I will get the money and repay your three thousand and farewell, woman of great wrath, but farewell, too, my love! Let us make an end! To-morrow I shall try and get it from everyone, and if I can’t borrow it, I give you my word of honor I shall go to my father and break his skull and take the money from under the pillow, if only Ivan has gone. If I have to go to Siberia for it, I’ll give you back your three thousand. And farewell. I bow down to the ground before you, for I’ve been a scoundrel to you. Forgive me! No, better not forgive me, you’ll be happier and so shall I! Better Siberia than your love, for I love another woman and you got to know her too well to-day, so how can you forgive? I will murder the man who’s robbed me! I’ll leave you all and go to the East so as to see no one again. Not _her_ either, for you are not my only tormentress; she is too. Farewell! P.S.—I write my curse, but I adore you! I hear it in my heart. One string is left, and it vibrates. Better tear my heart in two! I shall kill myself, but first of all that cur. I shall tear three thousand from him and fling it to you. Though I’ve been a scoundrel to you, I am not a thief! You can expect three thousand. The cur keeps it under his mattress, in pink ribbon. new: FATAL KATYA: Tomorrow I will get the money and repay your three thousand and farewell, woman of great wrath, but farewell, too, my love! Let us make an end! Tomorrow I will try to get it from everyone, and if I can’t borrow it, I give you my word of honor I will go to my father and break his skull and take the money from under the pillow, if only Ivan has gone. If I have to go to Siberia for it, I’ll give you back your three thousand. And farewell. I bow down to the ground before you, for I’ve been a scoundrel to you. Forgive me! No, better not forgive me, you’ll be happier and so will I! Better Siberia than your love, for I love another woman and you got to know her too well today, so how can you forgive? I will murder the man who’s robbed me! I’ll leave you all and go to the East so as to see no one again. Not _her_ either, for you are not my only tormentress; she is too. Farewell! old: After his talk with Alyosha, Ivan stood with his hand on the bell of his lodging and suddenly decided to go to Smerdyakov. He was acting on a sudden, odd impulse of indignation. He had just remembered how Katerina Ivanovna had cried out to him in Alyosha’s presence: “It was you, you, who convinced me of his” (that is, Mitya’s) “guilt!” Recalling it, Ivan was thunderstruck. He had never once tried to convince her that Mitya was the murderer. On the contrary, he had accused himself in front of her, that time when he came back from Smerdyakov. It was _she_, she, who had produced that “document” and proved his brother’s guilt. And now she had suddenly exclaimed: “I’ve been at Smerdyakov’s myself!” When had she been there? Ivan had known nothing about it. So she was not at all so sure of Mitya’s guilt! And what could Smerdyakov have told her? What, what had he said to her? His heart burned with violent anger. He could not understand how, half an hour before, he had let those words go by and not cried out on the spot. He let go of the bell and rushed off to Smerdyakov. “This time I may kill him,” he thought on the way.

old: “What is there left to tell? I was lying there, and I thought I heard the master shout. Just before that, Grigory Vassilyevitch had suddenly got up and gone out, and then he let out a scream, and after that it was all silent and dark. I lay there waiting, my heart thumping. I couldn’t stand it. In the end I got up and went out. The window on the left, the one facing the garden, was standing open. I stepped over to the left and listened for whether he was sitting in there alive, and I heard the master moving about and sighing. So I knew he was alive. ‘Ech!’ I thought. I went up to the window and called to him, ‘It’s me.’ And he called back, ‘He’s been here, he’s been here; he’s run off.’ He meant Dmitri Fyodorovitch had been. ‘He’s killed Grigory!’ ‘Where?’ I whispered. ‘There, in the corner,’ he said, and pointed. He was whispering too. ‘Wait a bit,’ I said. I went to the corner of the garden to look, and there was Grigory Vassilyevitch, lying by the wall, covered in blood and out cold. So it’s true, I thought, Dmitri Fyodorovitch really has been here. And on the spot I decided to put an end to it all. Grigory Vassilyevitch, even if he was alive, would never know what happened, lying there senseless like that. The one danger was that Marfa Ignatyevna might wake up. I felt that at the time. But the longing to get it done had come over me so badly that I could scarcely breathe. I went back to the window and told the master, ‘She’s here, she’s come; Agrafena Alexandrovna has come and wants to be let in.’ And he jumped like a baby. ‘Where is she?’ he gasped, but he couldn’t believe it. ‘She’s standing out there,’ I said. ‘Open up.’ He looked out of the window at me, half believing and half suspicious, and afraid to open. ‘Why, he’s afraid of me now,’ I thought. And it struck me as funny. So I thought of knocking on the window frame, right there before his eyes, with those taps we had agreed on as the sign that Grushenka had come. He didn’t seem to trust my word, but the moment he heard the taps, he ran to open the door. He opened it. I would have gone in, but he stood in the doorway so I couldn’t get past. ‘Where is she? Where is she?’ He stared at me, shaking all over. ‘Well,’ I thought, ‘if he’s that frightened of me, it looks bad!’ And my legs went weak with fear that he wouldn’t let me in, or would shout, or that Marfa Ignatyevna would come running, or that something else would go wrong. I can’t remember now, but I must have stood there pale, facing him. I whispered to him, ‘Why, she’s there, right under the window; how can you not see her?’ ‘Bring her, then, bring her.’ ‘She’s scared,’ I said; ‘the noise frightened her, she’s hiding in the bushes; go and call her yourself from the study.’ He ran to the window and put the candle on the sill. ‘Grushenka,’ he cried, ‘Grushenka, are you there?’ He cried it, but he wouldn’t lean out of the window, and he wouldn’t step away from me, because he was in a panic. He was so frightened he didn’t dare turn his back on me. ‘Why, there she is,’ I said. I went up to the window and leaned right out. ‘There she is; she’s in the bush, laughing at you, can’t you see her?’ All at once he believed it. He was shaking all over—he was terribly crazy about her—and he leaned right out of the window. I snatched up the iron paperweight from his table; you remember it, about three pounds in weight? I swung it and struck him on the top of the skull with the corner. He didn’t even cry out. He just sagged down, and I struck him again, and a third time. By the third blow I knew I had broken his skull. He suddenly rolled over on his back, face up, covered in blood. I looked myself over. There was no blood on me, not a spot. I wiped the paperweight and put it back. Then I went to the ikons, took the money out of the envelope, and dropped the envelope on the floor with the pink ribbon next to it. I went out into the garden, shaking all over, straight to the apple tree with the hollow in it—you know the hollow. I’d marked it long before and left a rag and a scrap of paper ready inside. I wrapped all the notes in the rag and shoved it deep into the hole. And there it stayed for over two weeks. I took it out afterwards, when I came out of the hospital. I went back to my bed and lay down, thinking, ‘If Grigory Vassilyevitch has been killed outright, it may turn out badly for me. But if he’s not killed and he recovers, it’ll be first-rate, because then he’ll swear that Dmitri Fyodorovitch was here, and so Dmitri Fyodorovitch must have killed him and taken the money.’ Then I began to groan, from suspense and impatience, to wake Marfa Ignatyevna as soon as I could. At last she got up and ran to me, but when she saw that Grigory Vassilyevitch wasn’t there, she ran out, and I heard her scream in the garden. That set it all in motion, and it put my mind at rest.”

old: “Listen ...” said Ivan, who seemed bewildered again and was struggling to catch hold of something. “Listen. There are many questions I wanted to ask you, but I’ve forgotten them ... I keep forgetting, and I get muddled. Yes. Tell me this, at least. Why did you tear open the envelope and leave it lying on the floor? Why didn’t you just carry the envelope off?... When you were telling me, you spoke of it as if it were the right thing to do ... but why, I can’t understand....”

old: “Why shouldn’t he, if he sometimes takes on fleshly form? I take on fleshly form and I take the consequences. Satan _sum et nihil humanum a me alienum puto_.”

old: “Shut your mouth, or I’ll kill you!”
new: “Be quiet, or I’ll kill you!”

old: Alyosha, as soon as he arrived, told Ivan that a little more than an hour before, Marya Kondratyevna had come running to his rooms with the news that Smerdyakov had killed himself. “I went in to clear away the samovar, and there he was, hanging from a nail in the wall.” Alyosha had asked whether she had told the police. She said she had told nobody, “but I flew straight to you, I ran the whole way.” She seemed to Alyosha completely out of her mind, and she was shaking like a leaf. He had hurried back with her to the cottage and found Smerdyakov still hanging there. On the table was a note: “I am ending my life of my own will and desire, so as to put no blame on anyone.” Alyosha had left the note where it lay, gone straight to the police captain and told him the whole story. “And from him I’ve come straight to you,” Alyosha concluded, looking hard into Ivan’s face. All through his account he had kept his eyes on Ivan, as though something in his expression had startled him.

old: “Yes, but he’s spiteful. He laughed at me. He was insolent, Alyosha,” said Ivan, shuddering with injured pride. “And he wronged me, wronged me in lots of ways. He told lies about me to my face. ‘Oh, you’re about to perform an act of heroic virtue: you’ll confess that you murdered your father, that the valet killed him at your instigation.’”

old: Some of the ladies, particularly those from out of town, showed up in the gallery very smartly dressed. But most of them had stopped thinking about clothes at all. Their faces showed a feverish, intense, almost unhealthy curiosity. One odd fact, which many observations confirmed afterwards, was that nearly all the ladies, or at least the vast majority, were on Mitya’s side and wanted him acquitted. This was perhaps mainly because he was known as a conqueror of women’s hearts. People knew that two women who were rivals would take part in the case. One of them, Katerina Ivanovna, was the center of general interest. All kinds of extraordinary stories went around about her, amazing anecdotes about her passion for Mitya in spite of his crime. People especially stressed her pride and her “aristocratic connections” (she had visited hardly anyone in the town). They said she meant to ask the Government for permission to follow the criminal to Siberia and marry him somewhere in the mines. Grushenka’s appearance in court was awaited with just as much impatience. The public looked forward with anxious curiosity to the meeting of the two rivals, the proud aristocratic girl and “the hetaira.” But the ladies of the district knew Grushenka better than they knew Katerina Ivanovna. They had already seen “the woman who ruined Fyodor Pavlovitch and his unhappy son.” Almost every one of them wondered how father and son could be so in love with “such a very common, ordinary Russian girl, who wasn’t even pretty.”

old: “Allow me to ask,” the counsel for the defense began, with the friendliest and even a respectful smile, “whether you are the same Mr. Rakitin whose pamphlet, _The Life of the Deceased Elder, Father Zossima_, I have just read with such pleasure. It was published by the diocesan authorities, it is full of deep and religious reflections, and it begins with an excellent, devout dedication to the bishop.”

old: “He once spoke to me of his hatred for our father, and of his fear that at an extreme moment ... in a moment of fury, he might murder him.”

old: “Quite so, nuts, I say so.” The doctor repeated it in the calmest way, as though he had never been at a loss for the word. “And I bought him a pound of nuts, for no one had ever bought the boy a pound of nuts before. And I lifted my finger and said to him, ‘Boy, _Gott der Vater_.’ He laughed and said, ‘_Gott der Vater_.’... ‘_Gott der Sohn_.’ He laughed again and lisped, ‘_Gott der Sohn_.’ ‘_Gott der heilige Geist_.’ Then he laughed and said as best he could, ‘_Gott der heilige Geist_.’ I went away, and two days after I happened to be passing, and he shouted to me by himself, ‘Uncle, _Gott der Vater, Gott der Sohn_,’ and he had only forgotten ‘_Gott der heilige Geist_.’ But I reminded him of it, and I felt very sorry for him again. But he was taken away, and I did not see him again. Twenty-three years passed. I am sitting one morning in my study, a white-haired old man, when there walks into the room a blooming young man I should never have known, but he held up his finger and said, laughing, ‘_Gott der Vater, Gott der Sohn_, and _Gott der heilige Geist_. I have just arrived and have come to thank you for that pound of nuts, for no one else ever bought me a pound of nuts; you are the only one that ever did.’ And then I remembered my happy youth and the poor child in the yard, with no boots on his feet, and my heart was touched and I said, ‘You are a grateful young man, for you have remembered all your life the pound of nuts I bought you in your childhood.’ And I embraced him and blessed him. And I shed tears. He laughed, but he shed tears, too ... for the Russian often laughs when he ought to be weeping. But he did weep; I saw it. And now, alas!...”

old: So Alyosha’s cross-examination came to an end. What mattered about it, and what struck everyone, was that at least one fact had come to light. It was only one tiny scrap, a mere hint of evidence, but it went some small way toward proving that the bag had really existed and had held fifteen hundred roubles. It suggested that the prisoner had not been lying at the preliminary inquiry when he claimed at Mokroe that the fifteen hundred roubles were “his own.” Alyosha was glad. With a flushed face he went back to the seat set aside for him. He kept repeating to himself: “How was it I forgot? How could I have forgotten it? And what made it come back to me now?”

old: No, I can never forget those moments. She began telling her story. She told everything, the whole episode that Mitya had told Alyosha, her bowing to the ground, and her reason for it. She told about her father and how she went to Mitya. Not in one word, not in a single hint, did she let on that Mitya himself, through her sister, had suggested that they “send Katerina Ivanovna” to fetch the money. She generously kept that back, and she was not ashamed to make it seem that she had run to the young officer on her own impulse, counting on something ... to beg him for the money. It was something tremendous! I went cold and trembled as I listened. The court was hushed, straining to catch each word. It was something without precedent. Even from a girl as willful and scornfully proud as she was, such a frank confession, such a sacrifice, such self-destruction, seemed unbelievable. And for what, and for whom? To save the man who had deceived and insulted her, and to help, however little, in saving him, by making a strong impression in his favor. And indeed, the figure of the young officer who, with a respectful bow to the innocent girl, handed her his last four thousand roubles, all he had in the world, was cast in a very sympathetic and attractive light. But ... I had a painful misgiving in my heart! I felt that slander might come of it later (and it did, in fact, it did). All over town afterwards it was repeated, with spiteful laughter, that the story was perhaps not quite complete, that is, in the statement that the officer had let the young lady leave “with nothing but a respectful bow.” People hinted that something had been left out here.

To save the man who had deceived and insulted her, and to help, however little, in saving him, by making a strong impression in his favor. And indeed, the figure of the young officer who, with a respectful bow to the innocent girl, handed her his last four thousand roubles, all he had in the world, was cast in a very sympathetic and attractive light. But ... I had a painful misgiving in my heart! I felt that slander might come of it later (and it did, in fact, it did). All over town afterwards it was repeated, with spiteful laughter, that the story was perhaps not quite complete, that is, in the statement that the officer had let the young lady leave “with nothing but a respectful bow.” People hinted that something had been left out here.

old: This came as a complete surprise to everyone. Nobody in the town or the monastery, not even Mitya, had known it. I was told that Rakitin went purple with shame where he sat. Somehow Grushenka had heard, before she came into court, that he had testified against Mitya, and that was why she was angry. Rakitin’s speech, with its noble sentiments and its attacks on serfdom and on the political disorder of Russia, had made an impression on the public. Now that effect was finally spoiled. Fetyukovitch was pleased: it was another godsend. Grushenka’s cross-examination was short, and of course her evidence could hold nothing especially new. She left a very unpleasant impression on the public. Hundreds of scornful eyes followed her as she finished her evidence and sat down again in the courtroom, a good way from Katerina Ivanovna. Mitya said nothing all through her evidence. He sat as though turned to stone, with his eyes on the floor.

old: Hardly anyone noticed him come in. The main witnesses, above all the two rival ladies, had already been questioned. For the time being curiosity was satisfied, and the public was almost worn out. Several more witnesses were still to be heard, and after all that had been said they probably had little to add. The time was passing. Ivan walked up with extraordinary slowness. He looked at no one, and he kept his head bowed, as if he were sunk in gloomy thought. His clothes were impeccable, but his face made a painful impression, on me at least. It looked earthy, like the face of a dying man. His eyes were dull. He lifted them and slowly looked around the court. Alyosha jumped up from his seat and moaned, “Ah!” I remember that, but hardly anyone noticed.

old: “I got it the day before the crime was committed, but he wrote it the day before that, at the tavern—that is, two days before he committed the crime. Look, it’s written on some kind of bill!” she cried breathlessly. “He hated me at that time. He had behaved contemptibly and was running after that creature ... and he owed me that three thousand.... Oh! That three thousand humiliated him, because of his own meanness! This is how it came about, that three thousand. I beg you, I implore you, listen to me. Three weeks before he murdered his father, he came to me one morning. I knew he needed money, and I knew what he wanted it for. Yes, yes—to win that creature and carry her off. I knew then that he had been false to me and meant to abandon me. And it was I, I, who gave him that money. I offered it to him on the pretext that he should send it to my sister in Moscow. And as I handed it over, I looked him in the face and said he could send it whenever he liked, ‘in a month’s time would do.’ How, how could he fail to understand that I was practically telling him to his face, ‘You want money to be false to me with your creature, so here is the money. I’m giving it to you myself. Take it, if you have so little honor as to take it!’ I wanted to prove what he was, and what happened? He took it, he took it, and squandered it with that creature in one night.... But he knew, he knew that I knew all about it. I assure you he understood, too, that I gave him that money to test him, to see whether he had lost every scrap of honor and would take it from me. I looked into his eyes and he looked into mine, and he understood it all, and he took it—he carried off my money!”

old: “Gentlemen of the jury,” began the prosecutor, “this case has caused a stir all over Russia. But why should that surprise us? What is so especially horrifying in it for us? We are so used to such crimes! That is what is truly horrible: that such dark deeds no longer horrify us. What ought to horrify us is that we have grown so used to them, and not this or that single crime. What are the causes of our indifference, of our lukewarm attitude toward such deeds, toward such signs of the times, which point to an unenviable future? Is it our cynicism? Is it the premature exhaustion of mind and imagination in a society that is sinking into decay in spite of its youth? Is it that our moral principles are shattered to their foundations, or perhaps that we have no such principles at all? I cannot answer such questions. Yet they are disturbing, and every citizen not only must, but ought to be troubled by them. Our newborn and still timid press has already done the public good service, for without it we would never have heard of the horrors of unbridled violence and moral degradation that the press keeps bringing to the notice, not only of those who attend the new jury courts set up in the present reign, but of everyone. And what do we read almost every day? Of things beside which the present case grows pale and seems almost commonplace. But what matters most is that the majority of our national crimes of violence bear witness to a widespread evil, now so general among us that it is hard to fight against it.

old: “Then he met a young girl of lofty character and brilliant education. Oh, I do not venture to repeat the details; you have only just heard them. There was honor there, and self-sacrifice, and I will say no more. The young officer, frivolous and profligate, paying homage to true nobility and a lofty ideal, showed himself to us in a very sympathetic light. But the other side of the coin was turned toward us without warning right afterwards, in this very court. Again I will not venture to guess why it happened so, but there were reasons. The same lady, in tears of long-concealed indignation, stated that he, of all men, had despised her for her action. That action was rash, even reckless perhaps, but it was still prompted by lofty and generous motives. He, the girl’s betrothed, looked at her with that smile of mockery, which was harder to bear from him than from anyone. And knowing that he had already deceived her (he had deceived her, believing that she was bound to put up with anything from him, even betrayal), she purposely offered him three thousand roubles. She made it clear, too clear, that she was offering him the money so that he would deceive her. ‘Well, will you take it or not? Have you no shame left?’ was the silent question in her piercing eyes. He looked at her and saw plainly what she was thinking (he has admitted before you that he understood it all). He took that three thousand without any conditions, and squandered it in two days with his new sweetheart.

old: Here Ippolit Kirillovitch turned to a detailed account of all Mitya’s attempts to borrow the money. He described the visit to Samsonov and the journey to Lyagavy. “Harassed, jeered at, hungry, he had sold his watch to pay for the journey (though he tells us he had fifteen hundred roubles on him, a likely story). He was tortured by jealousy at having left the object of his affections behind in the town, and he suspected she would go to Fyodor Pavlovitch while he was away. At last he came back to the town, and to his joy found that she had not gone near his father. He took her himself to her protector. (Strange to say, he does not seem to have been jealous of Samsonov, which is psychologically interesting.) Then he hurries back to his hiding place in the back gardens, and there he learns that Smerdyakov is in a fit and the other servant is ill. The coast is clear, and he knows the ‘signals.’ What a temptation! Still he resists it. He goes to see a lady who has lived in our town for some time and is highly respected among us, Madame Hohlakov. That lady had long followed his career with compassion. She gave him the most sensible advice: to give up his dissipated life, his unseemly love affair, and the waste of his youth and strength in pot-house debauchery, and to set off for the gold mines of Siberia. ‘That would be an outlet for your turbulent energy, your romantic character, your thirst for adventure.’”

old: “Karamazov had been frantically jealous of everyone. Yet before this first lover he simply collapsed and effaced himself on the spot. That makes it stranger still, since he seems to have given this formidable rival hardly a thought. He saw him as a danger far away, and Karamazov always lives in the present. Perhaps he took him for a fiction. But his wounded heart saw at once that the woman had been hiding this new rival from him and deceiving him. The man was anything but a fiction to her. He was the one hope of her life. The moment Karamazov grasped this, he gave in.

old: “Here we see, in excess, the love of effect, the romantic despair and sentimentality, and the wild recklessness of the Karamazovs. Yes, but there is something more, gentlemen of the jury, something that cries out in the soul, throbs without rest in the mind, and poisons the heart unto death. That _something_ is conscience, gentlemen of the jury, its verdict, its terrible torments! The pistol will settle everything, the pistol is the only way out! But _beyond_—I do not know whether Karamazov, at that moment, asked himself ‘What lies beyond?’ or whether a Karamazov could, like Hamlet, ask ‘What lies beyond?’ No, gentlemen of the jury, other nations have their Hamlets, but we still have our Karamazovs!”

old: “What need had he to be careful? Two or three times he came close to confessing. He hinted at it, he all but said it outright.” (Then came the witnesses’ evidence.) “He even shouted to the peasant who was driving him, ‘Do you know you are driving a murderer?’ But he could not speak out. He had to reach Mokroe and finish his romance there. And what was waiting for the luckless man? Almost from the first minute at Mokroe he saw that his unbeatable rival might not be so unbeatable after all, and that the toast to their new happiness was neither wanted nor welcome. But you know the facts, gentlemen of the jury, from the preliminary inquiry. Karamazov’s triumph over his rival was complete, and his soul entered a wholly new phase, perhaps the most terrible one it has passed through or ever will.

old: Ippolit Kirillovitch was genuinely moved, though he closed his speech with this rhetorical appeal. The effect was extraordinary. When he had finished, he hurried out and, as I have mentioned before, nearly fainted in the next room. There was no applause in the court, but the serious people were pleased. The ladies were less satisfied, although even they were pleased with his eloquence, particularly since they felt no anxiety about how the trial would end and had full faith in Fetyukovitch. “He will speak at last, and of course he will sweep everything before him.”

old: “There you have psychology. But let us take the same method and apply it to the case the other way round, and our result will be no less probable. The murderer, we are told, leapt down to find out, as a precaution, whether the witness was alive. Yet in his murdered father’s study he had left behind, as the prosecutor himself argues, an amazing piece of evidence: a torn envelope with an inscription saying that three thousand roubles had been in it. ‘If he had carried that envelope away with him, no one in the world would have known about the envelope and the notes in it, or that the prisoner had stolen the money.’ Those are the prosecutor’s own words. So on one side you see a complete lack of precaution. Here is a man who has lost his head and fled in a panic, leaving that clue on the floor. Two minutes later, when he has struck down another man, we are asked to assume in him the most heartless and calculating foresight. But even granting this, I suppose it is psychological subtlety that discovers that in some circumstances I become as bloodthirsty and sharp-eyed as a Caucasian eagle, while in the next I am as timid and blind as a mole. But if I am so bloodthirsty and so cruelly calculating that, having killed a man, I run back only to see whether he is alive to witness against me, why should I spend five minutes looking after my victim, at the risk of meeting other witnesses? Why soak my handkerchief wiping the blood from his head, so that it can be used as evidence against me later? If he were so cold-hearted and calculating, why not strike the servant again and again on the head with the same pestle, to kill him outright and be rid of all anxiety about the witness?

old: “The court has resolved to go on with the trial. Meanwhile, I would like to make a few remarks on the portrait of Smerdyakov that the prosecutor drew with such subtlety and talent. I admire his talent, but I cannot agree with him. I have visited Smerdyakov. I have seen him and talked with him, and he made quite a different impression on me. His health was weak, it is true. But in character, in spirit, he was far from the weak man the prosecutor has made of him. I found no sign of the timidity the prosecutor made so much of. Nor was he simple. On the contrary, I found a deep distrust of everyone, hidden behind a mask of _naïveté_, and a mind of considerable reach. The prosecutor was too simple himself in taking him for feeble-minded. He made a very definite impression on me, and I came away convinced that he was a plainly spiteful creature, wildly ambitious, vengeful, and intensely envious. I made some inquiries. He resented his birth and was ashamed of it, and he would grind his teeth when he remembered that he was the son of ‘stinking Lizaveta.’ He was disrespectful to the servant Grigory and his wife, who had looked after him in his childhood. He cursed Russia and sneered at it. He dreamed of going to France and becoming a Frenchman. He often used to say that he had not the money for it. I believe he loved no one but himself, and he held a strangely high opinion of himself. His whole notion of culture came down to good clothes, clean shirt-fronts and polished boots. He believed himself to be Fyodor Pavlovitch’s illegitimate son (there is evidence of this), and he might well have resented his position beside his master’s legitimate sons. They had everything, and he had nothing. They had every right, they had the inheritance, while he was only the cook. He told me himself that he had helped Fyodor Pavlovitch put the notes into the envelope. The purpose of that sum—a sum that would have made his career—must have been hateful to him. Besides, he saw three thousand roubles in new rainbow-colored notes. (I asked him about that on purpose.) Oh, beware of showing an ambitious and envious man a great sum of money all at once! And it was the first time he had seen so much money in one man’s hands. The sight of those rainbow-colored notes may have left a morbid mark on his imagination, but with no immediate result.

old: “The prosecutor asks at what moment Smerdyakov could have committed the murder. But it is very easy to name that moment. He might have woken out of a deep sleep (for he was only asleep—an epileptic fit is always followed by deep sleep) at the very moment when old Grigory shouted at the top of his voice, ‘Parricide!’ That shout in the dark and the silence may have woken Smerdyakov, whose sleep may by then have been lighter. He might quite naturally have been due to wake up an hour sooner.

If so, overwhelm him with your mercy! You will see, you will hear, how he trembles and is struck with horror. ‘How can I bear this mercy? How can I bear so much love? Am I worthy of it?’ That is what he will cry out.

old: “Next we are lectured that our tribune is a tribune of true and sound ideas, and from this tribune of ‘sound ideas’ a solemn declaration is made that calling the murder of a father ‘parricide’ is nothing but a prejudice! But if parricide is a prejudice, and if every child is to ask his father why he should love him, what will become of us? What will become of the foundations of society? What will become of the family? Parricide, it seems, is only a bogy for Moscow merchants’ wives. The most precious and most sacred guarantees for the destiny and future of Russian justice are laid before us in a twisted and frivolous form, all to reach a single aim—to justify something that cannot be justified. ‘Oh, crush him with mercy,’ cries the counsel for the defense. But mercy is all the criminal wants, and tomorrow we will see how crushed he is. And is the counsel for the defense not too modest in asking only that the prisoner be acquitted? Why not found a charity in honor of the parricide, to keep his exploit in memory for generations to come? Religion and the Gospel are corrected—all that is mysticism, we are told, and ours is the only true Christianity, the one that has been put to the test of reason and common sense. And so a false image of Christ is set up before us! ‘With the measure you use, it shall be measured to you again,’ cried the counsel for the defense, and he instantly concludes that Christ teaches us to measure as it is measured to us—and this from the tribune of truth and sound sense! We look into the Gospel only on the eve of making speeches, to dazzle the audience with our acquaintance with a book that is, at any rate, a rather original composition, and may be useful for creating a certain effect—all to serve our purpose! But what Christ commands us is something very different. He bids us beware of doing this, because the wicked world does it. We ought to forgive and to turn the other cheek, and not to measure out to our persecutors what they measure out to us. This is what our God has taught us. He did not teach us that forbidding children to murder their fathers is a prejudice. And we will not, from the tribune of truth and good sense, correct the Gospel of our Lord, Whom the counsel for the defense condescends to call only ‘the crucified lover of humanity,’ in defiance of all orthodox Russia, which cries out to Him, ‘For You are our God!’”
new: “Next we are lectured that our tribune is a tribune of true and sound ideas, and from this tribune of ‘sound ideas’ a solemn declaration is made that calling the murder of a father ‘parricide’ is nothing but a prejudice! But if parricide is a prejudice, and if every child is to ask his father why he should love him, what will become of us? What will become of the foundations of society? What will become of the family? Parricide, it seems, is only a bogy for Moscow merchants’ wives. The most precious and most sacred guarantees for the destiny and future of Russian justice are laid before us in a twisted and frivolous form, all to reach a single aim—to justify something that cannot be justified. ‘Oh, crush him with mercy,’ cries the counsel for the defense. But mercy is all the criminal wants, and tomorrow we will see how crushed he is. And is the counsel for the defense not too modest in asking only that the prisoner be acquitted? Why not found a charity in honor of the parricide, to keep his exploit in memory for generations to come? Religion and the Gospel are corrected—all that is mysticism, we are told, and ours is the only true Christianity, the one that has been put to the test of reason and common sense. old: At this the President broke in and reined in the over-eager speaker. He begged him not to exaggerate, not to go beyond the proper limits, and so on, the way presidents always do in such cases. The audience was uneasy too. The public was restless, and there were even shouts of indignation. Fetyukovitch hardly answered at all. He only stepped up to the tribune, laid his hand on his heart and, in an offended voice, spoke a few dignified words. Once more he touched lightly and ironically on “romancing” and “psychology,” and at a fitting moment he quoted, “Jupiter, you are angry, therefore you are wrong.” This drew a burst of approving laughter from the audience, since Ippolit Kirillovitch was nothing like Jupiter. Next, _à propos_ of the charge that he was teaching the young generation to murder their fathers, Fetyukovitch declared with great dignity that he would not even reply. As for the prosecutor’s accusation of unorthodox opinions, Fetyukovitch hinted that this was a personal insinuation. He had expected, he said, to be safe in this court from charges “damaging to my reputation as a citizen and a loyal subject.” At those words the President stopped him as well, and Fetyukovitch ended with a bow, to a murmur of approval through the courtroom. And Ippolit Kirillovitch was, in the view of our ladies, “finished for good.”

old: “It would be shameful, disgraceful, not to acquit him!” cried the official. “Say he did murder him—there are fathers and fathers! Besides, he was in such a frenzy.... He may really have done nothing more than swing the pestle through the air and knock the old man down by accident. But it was a pity they dragged the valet in. That was just an absurd theory! If I’d been in Fetyukovitch’s place, I would have said it straight out: ‘He murdered him, but he isn’t guilty, hang it all!’”

old: “Of course he didn’t tell you. It was that plan of escape. He had explained the main idea to me three days earlier, and we started quarreling over it at once, and we went on for three days. We quarreled because he said that if Dmitri Fyodorovitch were convicted, he would get him abroad together with that creature. I was furious at once. I can’t tell you why, I don’t know myself why.... Oh, of course I was furious about that creature, and that she should go abroad with Dmitri, too!” Katerina Ivanovna exclaimed suddenly, her lips quivering with anger. “The moment Ivan Fyodorovitch saw I was furious about that woman, he decided I was jealous of Dmitri and still loved him. That is how our first quarrel started. I wouldn’t explain, and I couldn’t ask his forgiveness. I couldn’t bear that such a man could suspect me of still loving that ... when I had told him myself, long before, that I did not love Dmitri, that I loved no one but him! It was only my resentment of that creature that made me angry with him. Three days later, on the evening you came, he handed me a sealed envelope, which I was to open at once if anything happened to him. Oh, he saw his illness coming! He said the envelope held the details of the escape, and if he died or fell dangerously ill, I was to save Mitya, and only Mitya. Then he left me money, nearly ten thousand. Those are the banknotes the prosecutor mentioned in his speech, when he had heard from someone that Ivan had sent them to be changed. It struck me tremendously that Ivan Fyodorovitch had not given up on saving his brother, and that he trusted me with the plan of escape, even though he was still jealous of me and still sure I loved Mitya. Oh, that was a sacrifice! No, you can’t understand how great such self-sacrifice is, Alexey Fyodorovitch. I wanted to fall at his feet in reverence. But then it came to me that he would take it only as joy at the thought of Mitya being saved (and he certainly would have thought so!). The mere possibility of such an unjust thought in his head made me so angry that I lost my temper again. Instead of kissing his feet, I flew into a rage again! Oh, I am unhappy! It’s my character, my awful, unhappy character! Oh, you’ll see, I will end by driving him away, too, to some other woman who suits him better, as Dmitri’s did. But ... no, I couldn’t bear it, I would kill myself. And when you came in then, and I called out to you and told him to come back, the look of contempt and hatred he gave me enraged me so much that—do you remember?—I cried out to you that it was he, he alone, who had convinced me his brother Dmitri was a murderer! I said that spiteful thing on purpose, to hurt him again. He had never, never convinced me that his brother was a murderer. On the contrary, it was I who convinced him! Oh, my vile temper caused everything! I paved the way for that hideous scene at the trial. He wanted to prove to me that he was an honorable man, and that even if I loved his brother, he would not destroy him out of revenge or jealousy. So he came to the court ... I am the cause of it all, I alone am to blame!”

old: “It is possible and it must happen!” Alyosha began forcefully, growing more animated. “He needs you very much just now. I wouldn’t have brought it up and upset you if it weren’t necessary. He is ill, he is beside himself, and he keeps asking for you. He doesn’t want you so that he can make peace with you. He only wants you to come and show yourself at his door. So much has happened to him since that day. He understands that he has wronged you beyond measure. He doesn’t ask your forgiveness—‘It’s impossible to forgive me,’ he says himself—he only asks that you appear in his doorway.”

old: “So you will come,” Alyosha said firmly, seeing her tears. “I’ll go and tell him you’re coming soon.”
new: “So you will come,” Alyosha said firmly, seeing her tears. “I’ll go and tell him you’re coming right away.”

old: “Listen,” Alyosha began. “She will come, but I don’t know when. Maybe today, maybe in a few days, I can’t say. But she will come, that’s certain.”
new: “Listen,” Alyosha began. “She will come, but I don’t know when. Maybe today, maybe in a few days, I can’t say. But she will come, she will, that’s certain.”

old: “No, of course not ... Still, I’d like to die for all humanity. And disgrace—I don’t care a bit about that. Let our names perish! I respect your brother!”
new: “Of course ... I would like to die for all humanity. And as for disgrace, I don’t care about that—our names may perish. I respect your brother!”

old: “Ah, children, dear friends, don’t be afraid of life! Life is so good when you do something good and right!”
new: “Ah, children, ah, dear friends, don’t be afraid of life! Life is so good when you do something good and just!”
